PQC Detection and Remediation by Language and Compute

Monitoring for non-PQ connections and the changes needed for post-quantum TLS, by language, compute type and infrastructure component. Covers simple cases, existing certificates in custom keystores, custom CA trust, mutual TLS and the other cases application teams meet.

Final edition, 2026-11-14. 22 sections: Overview, Runbook, five language tabs, twelve infrastructure tabs, Enforcement and guardrails, and the Configuration file index.

Overview

Summary

Outbound TLS becomes post-quantum (PQ) only when the client's TLS library offers the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3. Whether it does depends on the language runtime and its crypto library, not on the compute type. Compute type decides two other things: how you can see non-PQ connections, and how the fix ships.

  • Detection differs by compute type. Lambda and Fargate cannot be packet-mirrored, so they rely on AWS logs and app-side telemetry. Containers on EC2 can also use passive sensors.
  • Remediation differs by language and version. Some need only a config file, some a Java agent or library shim, and some a runtime or toolchain upgrade.
  • Every change ships through build, package and release. Configuration changes are released like code here, so the fix rides a shared build template, not per-function edits.

How to read the evidence labels in the tables:

Label Meaning
Tested Run between 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-16 in AWS Lambda base images under the local Runtime Interface Emulator, in official language and distro container images, or in the LocalStack end-to-end suite (e2e/), against a server that accepts only X25519MLKEM768. Not run on real AWS
Documented Stated in vendor documentation, not tested here
Claimed Stated by a vendor or third party as a plan or roadmap item, not yet shipped or confirmed
Unverified Believed true, no source opened or test run; confirm before relying on it

Detection: finding non-PQ connections

Use two kinds of signal together: posture (what a workload will negotiate, predicted from its runtime, versions and config) and observed (what a handshake actually negotiated, from logs or sensors). Posture covers everything you can inventory, including Lambda and Fargate, which can't be packet-mirrored. Observed signals confirm the fix and catch what posture misses, such as libraries that pin their own groups.

Observed signals by compute type

Compute type Calls to AWS APIs Calls to other services (internal, SaaS, internet) Inbound traffic Packet capture possible?
Lambda CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange per call, for KMS, STS, IAM, Secrets Manager and ACM only; other services log version and cipher (Documented) No AWS log shows the group. Options: route VPC-attached egress through a sensor appliance, or log from the client library Front door logs (row below) No
Fargate (ECS or EKS) CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange Same gap as Lambda; an egress proxy or sensor appliance in the VPC path Front door logs No. VPC Traffic Mirroring does not support Fargate (Documented)
Containers on EC2 (ECS, EKS, self-managed) and plain EC2 CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange Zeek 7.2+ on VPC Traffic Mirroring logs the negotiated group in ssl.log field curve. Node-level eBPF agents are possible but young Front door logs plus mirroring Yes, Nitro instance ENIs
Front doors: ALB, NLB, CloudFront, API Gateway n/a n/a ALB connection logs and NLB access logs record the key exchange (Documented). CloudFront passes CloudFront-Viewer-TLS-Details to the origin, including the key exchange (Documented) n/a
IoT devices on AWS IoT Core n/a n/a IoT Core has no PQ security policy, so every device connection is classical today (Documented). Inventory devices by firmware and TLS library n/a

Posture signals by compute type

Compute type Inventory source What to read
Lambda lambda list-functions across accounts, or AWS Config Runtime identifier, PackageType (zip or image), OPENSSL_CONF, JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, GODEBUG, attached layers. Classify with the matrix in the next section
Fargate and EC2 containers ECR images, task definitions, pod specs; an SBOM per image (Amazon Inspector SBOM export, Unverified) OS OpenSSL version, Go toolchain and go.mod version (go version -m <binary>), JDK version, Node version, Python's linked OpenSSL, env vars in the task definition
EC2 hosts SSM Inventory OS and OpenSSL version, crypto policy (update-crypto-policies --show)
Front doors AWS Config ELB and API Gateway security policy names; Config rule elbv2-predefined-security-policy-ssl-check takes an allowlist of PQ policy names

One rule holds for every row: a TLS 1.2 connection is always non-PQ, so tlsDetails.tlsVersion or the logged protocol is enough to flag it.

CloudTrail records keyExchange only for KMS, STS, IAM, Secrets Manager, ACM and Payment Cryptography so far; AWS lists it as coming soon for S3, DynamoDB, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, ECR and Direct Connect. Systems Manager isn't on AWS's PQ readiness list at all. Details are on the AWS service endpoints page.

Remediation matrix: language by compute type

The language and version decide the fix; the compute type decides where the fix lives. On Lambda zip functions AWS owns the OS, so the fix is a config file, agent or shim shipped in the package. In containers you own the base image, so the fix is usually the image's OpenSSL, JDK or toolchain version. Lambda container images follow the container column.

Language and version Lambda managed runtime (zip) Containers you build (Fargate, ECS or EKS on EC2, Lambda images) Evidence
Python 3.12, 3.13, 3.14 Ship openssl-pq.cnf in the package and set OPENSSL_CONF to it. Keeps the AL2023 crypto policy, adds the PQ group Debian 13 and Alpine 3.24 (OpenSSL 3.5) are PQ by default; Debian 12, Ubuntu 24.04 and Azure Linux 3.0 are not. On AL2023: update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:PQ in the Dockerfile, or the same config file. Python 3.15 adds SSLContext.set_groups() for code that must pin groups Tested
Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11 Runtime runs on AL2 with OpenSSL 1.1.1. Upgrade to 3.12+, or ship the urllib3/botocore shim (covers requests and boto3 only). Libraries that bundle their own TLS (next row) are already PQ here Not blocked: Python 3.11 on an AL2023 image links OpenSSL 3.5 and works with the config file Tested
Python libraries with bundled TLS: grpcio, awscrt, confluent-kafka, psycopg[binary], psycopg2-binary, pyOpenSSL Nothing beyond a current wheel: PQ on every Python runtime, including 3.9 to 3.11 on AL2. OPENSSL_CONF does not affect them Same, on any base image including Debian 12 Tested (grpcio 1.85.1, awscrt 0.38.1, psycopg 3.3.9)
Node.js 22.20+, 24.5+ (policy floor 24.9+, as AWS states) Ship openssl-pq-node.cnf and set OPENSSL_CONF. The Lambda bootstrap's own config removes the PQ group, so an override is required. Alternatives: NODE_OPTIONS=--openssl-config=..., OPENSSL_CONF=/dev/null, or tls.DEFAULT_ECDH_CURVE in code Official node images and tarballs: PQ by default (bundled OpenSSL 3.5), unless the image sets OPENSSL_CONF. Distro Node follows the system OpenSSL: AL2023 dnf install nodejs22 stays classical until DEFAULT:PQ Tested (Lambda, images, 24.5.0 and 24.9.0); floor Documented
Node.js 18, 20 No in-process fix: bundled OpenSSL has no ML-KEM. Upgrade the runtime; interim, the pq-egress extension (Tested in e2e) Upgrade Node, or use a distro Node linked to a system OpenSSL 3.5 (Debian 13's Node 20 and AL2023's dnf install nodejs20 negotiated PQ, the AL2023 one after DEFAULT:PQ or OPENSSL_CONF). Don't put X25519MLKEM768 first in ecdhCurve on the bundled Node 20: it crashes Tested (Lambda, Debian 13)
Java 8, 11, 17, 21 Ship the Bouncy Castle JSSE agent jar and set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:.... Java 8 also needs -Djdk.tls.client.protocols=TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2 (on Lambda) and -Dorg.bouncycastle.jsse.client.assumeOriginalHostName=true (everywhere; the pq-tls layer adds both). Servers with an EC certificate also need ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm=PKIX (kit v2 sets it) Same agent, or a static java.security BCJSSE entry (17, 21). Without Bouncy Castle: Netty tcnative-boringssl 2.0.85, or AWS SDK v2 CRT client (PQ in 2.59.1; CRT bundled with 2.35.10 was classical). Or move to JDK 25.0.5+. Oracle plans backports to 21 and 17 in H1 2027 (Claimed) Tested on java8.al2023, java8.al2, java11 and java17 (AL2) and java21; the newer java11.al2023 and java17.al2023 runtimes not tested (same JVM, other OS)
Java 25 (25.0.5+) Nothing: Corretto 25.0.5 negotiates PQ by default Corretto or Temurin 25.0.5+. JEP 527 targets JDK 27 but was backported to 25.0.5 (Oracle 25.0.5 release notes); other 25 builds need that update Tested (Lambda java25, Corretto and Temurin 25.0.5); backport Documented
Go Custom runtime (provided.al2023): build with Go 1.24+ and a go line of 1.24+ in go.mod, or set GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 Same; the base image doesn't matter, Go has its own TLS. FIPS mode: 1.24 no PQ; 1.25 X25519MLKEM768 only (fips140=only fails every handshake); 1.26+ adds the SecP hybrids. AWS SDK for Go v2 in FIPS mode forces P-256/384/521: re-add the hybrids with WithTransportOptions Tested 1.23 to 1.26, FIPS modes and the SDK fix
.NET 8, 10 Ship openssl-pq.cnf and set OPENSSL_CONF; .NET uses the OS OpenSSL 3.5 on Lambda Linux image with OpenSSL 3.5+ (Debian 13, Alpine, Ubuntu 26.04 resolute for .NET 10) or a PQ policy/config. .NET has no TLS group API, so the fix is OS-level only. Windows: Schannel group x25519_mlkem768, TLS 1.3 only, opt-in (Documented) Tested (Lambda dotnet8, dotnet10)
Rust Custom runtime: rebuild with rustls 0.23.x and the aws-lc-rs provider; AWS SDK for Rust crates published after 2025-08-29 default to PQ Same Documented (AWS SDK); rustls default version Claimed
Ruby, PHP Follow the system OpenSSL 3.5+; expected to behave like Python with the config file Same as Python Documented (AWS SDK guide); Lambda Unverified

Alternatives that change code or dependencies, for teams already editing a service:

  • AWS SDK for Java v2: the AWS CRT HTTP client negotiates PQ by default from 2.35.11, for AWS API calls only (Documented). Pin a tested version: 2.59.1 was PQ here, while the CRT shipped with 2.35.10 stayed classical (Tested).
  • Any language: explicitly configured group lists (Go CurvePreferences, Java jdk.tls.namedGroups, nginx ssl_ecdh_curve, Envoy ecdh_curves) silently stay classical until X25519MLKEM768 is added (Documented).
  • Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04 hosts and images: "PQ by default" covers programs linked to OpenSSL only. GnuTLS programs, such as wget and git over HTTPS (libcurl-gnutls), stay classical (Tested). GnuTLS has no ML-KEM group on Debian 13 (3.8.9), Debian 14 "forky" (3.8.13) or Ubuntu 26.04 (3.8.12); Fedora's 3.8.13 build lists five. Against a PQ-only server, Debian git fails with "GnuTLS, handshake failed", while Alpine git (libcurl on OpenSSL) connects. OpenSSH 10 defaults to mlkem768x25519-sha256 on all of them (Tested). Fix: use OpenSSL-linked tools (curl, Alpine or Fedora images) where the traffic matters, and count GnuTLS tools in posture.

Existing certificates, keystores and trust stores

Most application teams already load their own server certificates, client certificates and private CAs. PQ key exchange does not change certificates, so in almost every case nothing in the keystore or CA bundle has to change. Each language tab has a full case list (cases C, D and E), tested with the PQ fix in place. In summary:

Language Own server cert or keystore Own CA trust Mutual TLS What can still break
Go No change; tls.LoadX509KeyPair, GetCertificate and SNI work as before (Tested) No change; SSL_CERT_FILE replaces the default bundle rather than adding to it (Tested) No change (Tested) AWS_CA_BUNDLE with a plain *http.Client fails at config load: set RootCAs on the SDK's BuildableClient. x/crypto/pkcs12 can't read OpenSSL 3 PKCS#12 files
Python No change; load_cert_chain with RSA, EC or encrypted keys works (Tested) No change for cafile, certifi and REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE (Tested) No change (Tested) truststore.inject_into_ssl() disables the Lambda 3.9–3.11 shim for requests; gunicorn with an encrypted keyfile fails every worker (use an ssl_context hook); set_ecdh_curve or a TLS 1.2 maximum blocks PQ
Node.js No change for key/cert or modern PFX (Tested) No change for ca and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS (Tested) No change (Tested) Legacy RC2/3DES PFX files fail on every current runtime: re-export them. The Lambda image has an empty system CA store: set SSL_CERT_FILE
Java No change to JKS or PKCS#12 stores (Tested). With the Bouncy Castle agent, EC server certificates need the PKIX key manager (below) No change for cacerts or javax.net.ssl.trustStore (Tested) Works with kit v2; kit v1 silently sent no EC client cert (Tested) Code that hard-codes KeyManagerFactory.getInstance("SunX509") or Tomcat keyManagerAlgorithm="SunX509". RSA+EC stores serve EC to default clients
.NET No change for PFX, PEM or X509Store (Tested on Linux) No change for custom validation callbacks and CustomTrustStore (Tested) No change (Tested) X509Certificate2.CreateFromPemFile(caPath) throws on a CA-only file: use CreateFromPem(File.ReadAllText(path))

Java with the Bouncy Castle agent and an EC server certificate. Every handshake used to fail. The cause is the key manager, not the certificate: Bouncy Castle asks for key type EC/secp256r1, and the JDK default SunX509 key manager returns no alias for it. The fix is one security property, ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm=PKIX, in a file passed with -Djava.security.properties=<file> or added to java.security. Kit v2's agent sets it and ships pq-tls.security. With it, Tomcat 11.0.29, Jetty 12.1.15 and HttpsServer on JDK 17 and 21 negotiate X25519MLKEM768 with an EC certificate, and an X25519-only client still connects (Tested). Spring Boot 3.5.16 SSL bundles use the default algorithm and work. An app's own -Djava.security.properties overrides the kit file, so add the line there too. On JDK 25 with the default SunX509, the server ignored SNI on a two-certificate store; PKIX fixes that as well (Tested).

Per-language detail

Each entry gives the exact setting, what it covers, and how to check it worked. Lambda results for the AL2023 runtimes come from the AL2023.12.20261109 base images; python3.9 to 3.11, nodejs18.x, java8.al2, java11, java17 and provided.al2 run on Amazon Linux 2.

Python and .NET (system OpenSSL)

Both use the operating system's OpenSSL, so one config file serves both. It loads the AL2023 crypto policy and replaces only the group list:

openssl_conf = openssl_init
.include /etc/pki/tls/openssl.d
[openssl_init]
providers = provider_sect
ssl_conf = ssl_module
[provider_sect]
default = default_sect
[default_sect]
activate = 1
[ssl_module]
system_default = pq_system_default
[pq_system_default]
.include = /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensslcnf.config
Groups = *X25519MLKEM768:*X25519:secp256r1:X448:secp521r1:secp384r1:ffdhe2048:ffdhe3072:ffdhe4096:ffdhe6144:ffdhe8192
  • Set: OPENSSL_CONF=/var/task/pq-tls/openssl-pq.cnf.
  • Baseline check: with this file, Python 3.12's minimum TLS version, cipher list and options were identical to the default. OPENSSL_CONF=/dev/null also enables PQ but drops the crypto policy and changed the cipher list, so don't use it.
  • Python 3.9 to 3.11 on Lambda (AL2, OpenSSL 1.1.1): a sitecustomize.py shim patches urllib3 and botocore to use pyOpenSSL, whose bundled OpenSSL offers PQ. Set PYTHONPATH to the shim's directory. It covers requests and boto3, not ssl, http.client, aiohttp or httpx. It overrides a deliberate botocore choice; it was tested with certificate verification on against a private CA, including mutual TLS (e2e py-lambda-py39/310/311-*), but not against real AWS endpoints, so treat it as a bridge until the runtime upgrade. Build pyOpenSSL, cryptography and idna inside each Python version's Lambda image: without idna every request fails.
  • pq-egress Lambda extension (interim, Tested in the LocalStack e2e suite on every Lambda runtime: Python 3.9-3.14, Node 18-24, Java 8-25, dotnet8/10, Go 1.23 on provided.al2023/al2): an external extension that makes the outbound TLS connection with X25519MLKEM768 for a function whose runtime can't. The function sends plain HTTP to http://127.0.0.1:2779/<route>/<path> (routes in PQ_EGRESS_ROUTES, optional client certificate per route), so the app's base URL changes; the loopback hop never leaves the execution environment. Same pattern as the AWS Parameters and Secrets Lambda Extension. Source: e2e/lambda/extension/pq-egress/. Not tested for AWS SDK calls (SigV4 signs the host name) or on real AWS.

Node.js (bundled OpenSSL)

Node compiles in its own OpenSSL; 22.20+ and 24.5+ ship 3.5 (use 24.9+ as the policy floor, as AWS does). On Lambda the bootstrap sets OPENSSL_CONF=/var/runtime/openssl_conf/openssl.cnf, whose only setting is a group list without ML-KEM. The override is the same file with the PQ group added:

nodejs_conf = openssl_init
[openssl_init]
ssl_conf = ssl_sect
[ssl_sect]
system_default = system_default_sect
[system_default_sect]
Groups = *X25519MLKEM768:*X25519:secp256r1:X448:secp521r1:secp384r1:ffdhe2048:ffdhe3072:ffdhe4096:ffdhe6144:ffdhe8192
  • Set: OPENSSL_CONF=/var/task/pq-tls/openssl-pq-node.cnf.
  • Watch for drift: this file replaces AWS's rather than including it. Add a pipeline check that diffs AWS's file against ours, minus the PQ group.
  • Node 18 and 20: bundled OpenSSL is older than 3.5. No setting helps; upgrade.

Java (JSSE, independent of the OS)

Java's TLS stack doesn't use OpenSSL, so moving to AL2023 changes nothing for Java. JDKs before 25 have no ML-KEM groups.

  • Java 8 to 21: a Java agent (pq-tls-agent.jar, compiled for Java 8) registers Bouncy Castle 1.87 as the first JSSE provider and sets jdk.tls.namedGroups=X25519MLKEM768,x25519,secp256r1,secp384r1 unless already set. Set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS=-javaagent:/var/task/pq-tls/pq-tls-agent.jar.
  • Java 8 only: also add -Djdk.tls.client.protocols=TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2, since the Lambda Java 8 runtime limits clients to TLS 1.2, and -Dorg.bouncycastle.jsse.client.assumeOriginalHostName=true, without which Bouncy Castle rejects every HttpsURLConnection handshake ("No hostname specified for HTTPS endpoint ID check").
  • Why an agent: the Lambda Java bootstrap's system classpath is /var/runtime/lib only, so providers registered through java.security from other paths are silently ignored.
  • Risk: Bouncy Castle becomes the TLS provider for the whole process. Test functions that use custom keystores, FIPS mode or mutual TLS first.
  • Servers with an EC certificate: also set ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm=PKIX (kit v2's pq-tls.security, passed with -Djava.security.properties=). Without it every handshake fails. See "Existing certificates, keystores and trust stores" above.
  • Java 25: Corretto 25.0.5 negotiates PQ with the stock SunJSSE provider.

Go (own TLS stack)

  • Needs both: a Go 1.24+ toolchain and a go directive of 1.24+ in go.mod. A 1.25 build of a module whose go.mod says 1.23 stayed classical in testing.
  • No-code override: GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 turned that build PQ, and can be set in the deployment config.
  • Pitfall: code that sets tls.Config.CurvePreferences gets no PQ.

Rust

rustls with the aws-lc-rs provider supports X25519MLKEM768. Sources disagree on which 0.23.x release made it the default (0.23.22 or 0.23.27). The AWS SDK for Rust defaults to PQ for crates published after 2025-08-29. Rebuild with current crates; apps on the openssl crate follow the system OpenSSL instead.

Inbound: front doors and TLS 1.3 enforcement

Inbound connections become PQ when the front door's TLS policy offers ML-KEM and the caller supports it. Allow TLS 1.2 and 1.3 first, measure, then move each endpoint to TLS 1.3 only once its TLS 1.2 traffic reaches zero. TLS negotiation already picks 1.3 when both sides support it, and TLS 1.3's downgrade protection stops an attacker forcing 1.2.

Front door PQ setting Notes Evidence
ALB, NLB ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-2-Res-PQ-2025-09 (allows 1.2 and 1.3), later ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-3-PQ-2025-09 (1.3 only); FIPS variants exist Console default is a PQ policy, but CLI, CloudFormation and CDK default to ELBSecurityPolicy-2016-08. The backend leg also becomes PQ-capable: AWS then uses ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-0-PQ-2025-09 towards HTTPS targets, and the hop is PQ only when the target has its language fix (e2e target-leg cases, 2026-11-15; LocalStack can't test the listener leg itself). Enforce in an SCP with the elasticloadbalancing:SecurityPolicy condition key, which applies to CreateListener and ModifyListener (not CreateLoadBalancer) Documented
CloudFront Viewer side PQ by default on all policies Origin leg is classical; AWS says PQ is coming Documented
API Gateway REST (Regional, private) SecurityPolicy_TLS13_1_2_PQ_2025_09 and variants No TLS 1.3-only PQ policy exists. API Gateway egress to integrations is TLS 1.2 only, so that leg can never be PQ Documented
API Gateway HTTP, WebSocket, edge-optimized No PQ policy Front with CloudFront or ALB if PQ is required Documented (absence)
AWS IoT Core No PQ policy Every device leg classical until AWS adds one Documented (absence)
Service mesh (EKS) Linkerd 2.19+ PQ by default; Istio 1.27+ COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc (enforces PQ, breaks non-PQ peers) Covers mesh-owned legs only, not app-originated TLS Documented

Move legacy callers that can't do TLS 1.3 to a separate listener or hostname that still allows 1.2, tracked as exceptions, rather than holding the main endpoint open for them. The SCP and Config rules that hold this line are on the Enforcement and guardrails tab. Check exact policy names with aws elbv2 describe-ssl-policies before putting them in templates.

Rollout through build, package and release

Every change, including configuration, ships as a release here. So the fix lives in the shared build template, and each workload picks it up on its next release with no per-service code edits.

The loop has four steps, repeated every release cycle: Classify → Change request → Release → Verify.

The release step is the only one that changes a workload; the others are automation around it.

  1. Classify. The posture inventory sorts each workload into a matrix row and records the gap.
  2. Change request. A bot opens a pull request in each repo that bumps the shared module or template. The template ships the right files under /var/task/pq-tls/ (config file, agent jar or shim) and sets the matching variable. It leaves a workload's own OPENSSL_CONF alone and flags it for review. Bundling into the package avoids Lambda's 5-layer limit.
  3. Release. The normal pipeline builds, packages and releases. A guardrail (cfn-guard, OPA/conftest or a CloudFormation Hook) warns, then later fails, on Lambda and task definitions missing the PQ settings, and on non-PQ ELB policies.
  4. Verify. Observed signals confirm the workload's connections moved to PQ; shipping isn't proof. CLM tracks each workload as a campaign item.

Dormant workloads with no release coming: rank them by observed classical traffic. One making no classical outbound TLS doesn't need forcing; the rest get a no-op rebuild and release. Runtimes past AWS's block-update date can't be changed at all, so schedule those first.

Evidence and sources

Tests (2026-11-12). AWS Lambda base images under the Runtime Interface Emulator, against a Node 24 test server with one port accepting only X25519MLKEM768 and one accepting only X25519. Images: python 3.9 to 3.14, nodejs 18 to 24, java 8.al2023, 11, 17, 21, 25, dotnet 8 and 10, provided.al2023 with Go 1.23 to 1.25. Scripts and files are kept with the pq-tls test kit.

Tests (2026-11-15), end to end. 469 cases in LocalStack Pro (e2e/): real Lambda zip, layer, extension and image functions, ECS Fargate and ECS on EC2 tasks, and EC2 instances from AL2023 and AL2 AMIs, for all five languages, each graded against this document by a TLS observer, plus 32 load balancer target-leg cases. Results: e2e/results/latest/summary.md. Real AWS, x86_64 and the ALB/NLB listener leg were not covered.

Tests (2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14). Existing-certificate cases (own keystores and key files, private CA trust, mutual TLS, explicit TLS settings) for all five languages, in official language and distro images (Debian 12, 13 and 14, Ubuntu 26.04, Alpine, AL2023, Fedora) against OpenSSL 3.5 s_server instances that accept only X25519MLKEM768 or only X25519. The Bouncy Castle EC server fix was tested on Tomcat 11.0.29, Jetty 12.1.15 and HttpsServer, JDK 17, 21 and 25. Each language tab lists its scripts and results.

Runbook by language

Each language tab says, for each component, exactly what to change: the version to upgrade to, the file to ship, the variable to set, and how to check it worked. Every change goes through the normal build, package and release; nothing here is applied by hand.

Language tabs

Language What decides PQ Status today Main action

Python stdlib ssl follows the platform OpenSSL; some wheels bundle their own TLS Debian 13 and Alpine images PQ; Lambda and AL2023 need the config; grpcio, awscrt, psycopg binary, pyOpenSSL PQ everywhere Ship openssl-pq.cnf on Lambda/AL2023 or use an OpenSSL 3.5 image; shim or upgrade 3.9 to 3.11 on Lambda

Every language tab follows the same page template, built for application teams that already run services with their own certificates and TLS settings:

  1. Problem statement: what goes wrong today in this language, and who controls the handshake.
  2. Versions and native support: one row per runtime version line, with the TLS stack, PQ client and server defaults per compute type, the group API, FIPS behaviour, the proposed fix and an evidence label; then a short decision guide.
  3. Cases: what to change: A simple client, B simple server, C existing server certificates in a custom keystore or key files, D custom CA trust, E mutual TLS, F explicit TLS settings that block PQ, G FIPS mode, H libraries with their own TLS stack, I pinning and HSM or KMS keys, J other cases. Each case says who it applies to (with a grep), what happens today, what to change (often nothing), and side effects.
  4. Solution and automation: inventory, the change per compute type with IaC excerpts, CI guardrails, and canary rollout with rollback.
  5. How to test: numbered steps with full scripts: posture, a PQ-only and a classical-only test server, a test per case, the in-cloud signal, and the rollback test.
  6. Pitfalls and rollback.
  7. Full configuration files, also listed in Configuration file index.

Existing certificates and keystores: in every language the keystore, key files and CA bundles stay as they are; only the platform fix applies. The exceptions are listed per language in the Overview's "Existing certificates, keystores and trust stores" table, most importantly the PKIX key manager setting for Java servers with EC certificates under Bouncy Castle.

The kit is versioned once and pulled in by the shared build template, so a fix to a file reaches every workload on its next release.

Checking a workload

  • Observed: CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange for its AWS API calls shows X25519MLKEM768, and ELB logs show the same for inbound traffic.
  • Test endpoint: a test server that accepts only X25519MLKEM768 (openssl s_server -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 with OpenSSL 3.5) fails any client that isn't PQ. Each tab's verify step uses it.

Go

Problem statement

A Go service is classical when any one of these is true, and it says nothing about it: the binary was built with Go 1.23 or older, the main module's go line is below 1.24, code or a library sets CurvePreferences without a hybrid or caps TLS at 1.2, or FIPS mode runs on Go 1.24 or with boringcrypto fipsonly. The handshake still succeeds with X25519, so nothing breaks and no log shows it (Tested).

Go's own crypto/tls, compiled into the binary, controls the handshake. OpenSSL, the OS crypto policy, the base image and the Lambda runtime play no part. Five inputs decide the result: the toolchain version, the go line in go.mod (it sets DefaultGODEBUG), GODEBUG at run time, any tls.Config.CurvePreferences or MaxVersion in your code or a library, and FIPS 140-3 mode. Exceptions: the Microsoft build of Go and Red Hat's Go toolset can route crypto to OpenSSL in FIPS mode; their PQ behaviour was not tested.

The risk is harvest-now-decrypt-later: traffic recorded today under X25519 or P-256 key exchange can be decrypted once a large quantum computer exists. Hybrid X25519MLKEM768 removes that risk for new sessions. Certificates and keystores are a separate question (see Certificates (ML-DSA)).

Versions and native support

The binary carries its own TLS, so the answer is the same on Lambda (zip or image), ECS, Fargate, EKS and EC2 (Tested: identical results in public.ecr.aws/lambda/provided:al2023, distroless/static-debian12 and debian:trixie-slim).

Version TLS stack PQ client by default (all compute types) PQ server by default API to set groups FIPS-mode behaviour Proposed solution Evidence
1.27.x (supported) crypto/tls in the binary Yes, when go line ≥ 1.24: X25519MLKEM768; SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 when go ≥ 1.26 Yes, same rule CurvePreferences (an explicit list now beats tlsmlkem=0); GODEBUG tlsmlkem, tlssecpmlkem; opt-in MLKEM1024 fips140=on/only: the three hybrids + P-256, P-384, P-521 Keep; set go 1.26+ Tested (2026-11-14, first pass)
1.26.x (supported) same Yes, same rule as 1.27 Yes CurvePreferences; GODEBUG (tlsmlkem=0 beats an explicit list) Same as 1.27 Target. Build with 1.26+, go 1.26 Tested (this pass: cases C to I)
1.25.x (no security fixes since 1.27) same Yes if go ≥ 1.24, X25519MLKEM768 only Yes same as 1.26 on: X25519MLKEM768 + P-256, P-384, P-521; only: every handshake fails Upgrade to 1.26 Tested
1.24.x (unsupported) same Yes if go ≥ 1.24; No with go 1.22/1.23 (tlsmlkem=0) Same rule: a go 1.22 server refused a PQ-only client (Tested this pass) same on/only: P-256, P-384, P-521 only, no PQ Upgrade; interim GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 (Tested client and server) Tested
1.23 and older (unsupported) same No ML-KEM. 1.23 offers the pre-standard X25519Kyber768Draft00 (0x6399), which OpenSSL 3.5 PQ-only servers reject No tlskyber only No PQ Rebuild with 1.26 Tested (1.23.12; source crypto/tls/defaults.go)

Decision guide

  • go version -m <binary> shows go1.23 or older: rebuild with Go 1.26. Nothing else helps.
  • It shows tlsmlkem=0 in DefaultGODEBUG: raise the go line to 1.26. If you can't yet, add godebug tlsmlkem=1 to go.mod or set GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 in the function, task or pod.
  • Your code or a library sets CurvePreferences or MaxVersion: tls.VersionTLS12: fix it (case F).
  • You run FIPS mode: Go 1.26+ native FIPS (GOFIPS140), not boringcrypto (case G).
  • None of the above: you already negotiate X25519MLKEM768. Verify (How to test) and move on.

Detail: toolchain and go line

Client with default tls.Config, against one server per group (OpenSSL 3.5.7). Tested 2026-11-14, golang images pinned by digest, linux/arm64.

Toolchain go line in go.mod X25519MLKEM768 SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024 Classical server still works Evidence
1.27.4 1.27 Yes Yes Yes Tested
1.27.4 1.23 No (tlsmlkem=0) No Yes Tested
1.26.11 1.26 Yes Yes Yes Tested
1.26.11 1.25 Yes No (tlssecpmlkem=0) Yes Tested
1.26.11 1.23 No No Yes Tested
1.25.14 1.25 Yes No (added in 1.26) Yes Tested
1.25.14 1.23 No No Yes Tested
1.24.13 1.24 Yes No Yes Tested
1.24.13 1.23 No No Yes Tested
1.23.12 any No (no ML-KEM in 1.23) No Yes Tested

Pure MLKEM1024 is never offered by default. Go 1.27 offers it only when listed in CurvePreferences (Tested).

Compute type What to change Evidence
Lambda zip, provided.al2023 or provided.al2 Rebuild bootstrap; optional GODEBUG env var Tested: same binaries run in public.ecr.aws/lambda/provided:al2023 gave identical results
Lambda container image Rebuild the image (builder stage Go 1.26+) Tested (same image as above)
Fargate, ECS on EC2, EKS Rebuild the image; any base, including scratch and distroless Tested: e2e ECS Fargate and ECS on EC2 on scratch, distroless, golang and AL2023 images (go-fargate-*, go-ecsec2-*); EKS not run
EC2 (systemd, SSM-deployed binary) Redeploy the binary Tested: e2e EC2 from AL2023 and AL2 AMIs, including a systemd GODEBUG drop-in (go-ec2-*); no OS dependency (CGO_ENABLED=0)
go1.x managed Lambda runtime Retired; move to provided.al2023 Documented (AWS)

  1. Toolchain sets what exists: 1.24 added X25519MLKEM768; 1.26 added SecP256r1MLKEM768 and SecP384r1MLKEM1024 to the defaults; 1.27 added opt-in MLKEM1024 (Go 1.26, Go 1.27 notes; Tested).

  2. The go line in the main module's go.mod (or go.work) sets the defaults. Below 1.24 gives tlsmlkem=0; below 1.26 gives tlssecpmlkem=0. A dependency's go.mod doesn't count (Documented; Tested).

  3. Override without raising the go line: a godebug tlsmlkem=1 line in go.mod (Go 1.23+ toolchains), or //go:debug tlsmlkem=1 above package main. Both put tlsmlkem=1 into DefaultGODEBUG (Tested on 1.24 to 1.27). On 1.26+ add tlssecpmlkem=1 for the SecP hybrids (Tested).

  4. Run-time GODEBUG beats both: GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 turns PQ on with no rebuild; tlsmlkem=0 turns it off (Tested).

  5. Explicit CurvePreferences vs tlsmlkem=0. On 1.24 to 1.26, tlsmlkem=0 drops X25519MLKEM768 even from an explicit list. From 1.27 an explicit list wins (Documented; Tested both).

  6. Support window. Go supports the two newest majors, today 1.27 and 1.26 (release policy). Go 1.25 still works for X25519MLKEM768 but gets no security fixes.

Raising the go line changes other defaults too. Going to 1.27 removes tls10server, tlsrsakex, tls3des, tlsunsafeekm, x509keypairleaf and asynctimerchan, so run the service tests. The GODEBUG route changes only the TLS groups.

Cases: what to change

A. Simple client

Who this is. No TLS settings in your code: grep -rnE --include='*.go' 'tls\.Config|TLSClientConfig|CurvePreferences|MaxVersion' . finds nothing. You use http.Get, the AWS SDK default client, or a DB driver with a DSN.

What happens today. PQ when the toolchain and the go line are both 1.24+; classical otherwise (Tested, every library in the table below).

What to change. Nothing in code. Raise the go line and rebuild.

Side effects. The ClientHello grows by about 1.2 KB (see Pitfalls). Raising the go line changes other GODEBUG defaults too.

Rule for every library below: pass a tls.Config without CurvePreferences, or none at all. Tested with Go 1.26.11 (go 1.26) against a Go server that accepts only X25519MLKEM768 and logs the negotiated group.

Client Version tested Where TLS is set PQ by default Evidence
crypto/tls Dialer, tls.Dial stdlib tls.Config Yes Tested
net/http default client, DefaultTransport.Clone() stdlib Transport.TLSClientConfig Yes Tested
gRPC-go v1.85.0 credentials.NewTLS(cfg) Yes; it doesn't set CurvePreferences Tested (client to PQ-only gRPC server)
AWS SDK for Go v2 v1.48.0 awshttp.NewBuildableClient() Yes, outside FIPS mode Tested
AWS SDK for Go v2, FIPS 140-3 mode v1.48.0 same No: the SDK forces P-256/P-384/P-521 Tested; fix below
pgx (and database/sql via pgx/v5/stdlib) v5.13.0 sslmode=require/verify-full, ConnConfig.TLSConfig Yes Tested with sslnegotiation=direct
go-redis v9.23.0 Options.TLSConfig Yes Tested
segmentio/kafka-go v0.4.51 Dialer.TLS, Transport.TLS Yes Tested
IBM/sarama v1.61.1 Config.Net.TLS.Config Yes Tested
lib/pq, mongo-go-driver, others — their tls.Config Probably, if they don't set CurvePreferences Unverified: grep them (Verify)

Whether the far end accepts ML-KEM is a server question: see AWS service endpoints and Databases and data services.

net/http and crypto/tls. Nothing to set. If a team insists on an explicit list, keep the hybrids in it. Since Go 1.24 the order of CurvePreferences is ignored, so position doesn't matter (Documented).

tr := http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone()
tr.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12} // no CurvePreferences
client := &http.Client{Transport: tr}

// Only if a list is mandatory (Go 1.26+ constants):
cfg := &tls.Config{CurvePreferences: []tls.CurveID{
    tls.X25519MLKEM768, tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768, tls.X25519, tls.CurveP256}}

B. Simple server

Who this is. http.ListenAndServeTLS, or frameworks on top of net/http (chi, gin, echo), or a gRPC server with credentials.NewTLS, with no CurvePreferences.

What happens today. With 1.24+ and go ≥ 1.24, RSA and EC servers negotiate X25519MLKEM768 with a PQ client and X25519 with a classical one (Tested 1.24.13, 1.25.14, 1.26.11). A 1.24 build with go 1.22 refused a PQ-only client and served X25519 to others; GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 fixed it with no rebuild (Tested).

What to change. Nothing beyond the build. Side effects. None seen.

Server setup PQ client Classical client Evidence
net/http ListenAndServeTLS, default tls.Config X25519MLKEM768 and SecP256r1MLKEM768 negotiated Works (X25519, or P-256 on TLS 1.2) Tested, Go 1.26.11
CurvePreferences: {X25519, P256} (the pitfall) PQ-only client fails; hybrid-capable client silently falls back to X25519 Works Tested
PQ-only: MinVersion: TLS13, CurvePreferences: {X25519MLKEM768} Works Rejected; TLS 1.2 rejected Tested
gRPC server, credentials.NewTLS(default) X25519MLKEM768 with ALPN h2 Works Tested

Default server. Leave CurvePreferences nil and build with Go 1.26+ and go 1.26. The go line governs servers too: tlsmlkem=0 removes ML-KEM from the default list on both sides (Documented; server side Tested, see "What happens today" above).

srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8443", Handler: mux,
    TLSConfig: &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12}} // no CurvePreferences
log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("/etc/tls/tls.crt", "/etc/tls/tls.key"))

Behind an ALB or NLB TLS listener (e2e, 2026-11-15): with the load balancer modelled as the client on the target leg, a net/http target built with Go 1.26 and go 1.26 negotiated X25519MLKEM768 under the PQ backend policy; Go 1.23, and Go 1.26 with go 1.23, stayed classical until GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 was set in the task definition (cases srv-go-*, Load balancers tab).

C. Existing server certificates in your own files or keystore

Who this is. grep -rnE --include='*.go' 'LoadX509KeyPair|X509KeyPair|GetCertificate|pkcs12\.|DecryptPEMBlock|pkcs8\.' .

What happens today. The certificate store has no effect on key exchange. Every setup below negotiated X25519MLKEM768 with an OpenSSL 3.5.7 PQ-only client and X25519 with a classical client, as a server built with Go 1.24.13 (go 1.24), 1.25.14 and 1.26.11. With Go 1.23.12 or go 1.22 every row was classical, so the store was never the cause (all Tested).

Setup Code Which certificate is served Store change
RSA 2048 PEM pair tls.LoadX509KeyPair(crt, key) RSA None
EC P-256 PEM pair same EC None
RSA and EC together Certificates: {rsa, ec} Go serves the first certificate the client supports: RSA to a default client, EC only to an ECDSA-only client None; order picks the cert, not the group
EC and RSA together Certificates: {ec, rsa} EC to a default client, RSA to an RSA-only client None
Two hostnames Certificates: {a.test, b.test} Matched by SNI; unknown SNI gets the first None
Callback GetCertificate by ClientHelloInfo.ServerName Per SNI, with your fallback None
Legacy encrypted PEM (Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED) x509.DecryptPEMBlock then tls.X509KeyPair RSA None
Encrypted PKCS#8 (BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY) github.com/youmark/pkcs8 ParsePKCS8PrivateKey (1.26.11) EC None
PKCS#12, OpenSSL 3 default (AES-256-CBC, PBKDF2, SHA-256 MAC) with chain software.sslmate.com/src/go-pkcs12 v0.7.4 DecodeChain (1.26.11) EC None
PKCS#12, legacy 3DES/SHA-1 golang.org/x/crypto/pkcs12 v0.59.0 Decode (1.26.11) RSA None
Same x/crypto package on the OpenSSL 3 default file Decode Fails at load: pkcs12: unknown digest algorithm: 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1 Use go-pkcs12, or re-export the file
Cert and key PEM in env vars (ECS secrets, Lambda env) tls.X509KeyPair([]byte(os.Getenv(...))) RSA None

Encrypted keys. The Go standard library can't read encrypted PKCS#8, and x509.DecryptPEMBlock is deprecated because RFC 1423 encryption is insecure by design (Documented). What teams do instead, in order of preference:

  1. Keep the key unencrypted at rest inside a secret store (Secrets Manager, a Kubernetes Secret, the ECS secrets field), mount or inject it with tight permissions, and load it with tls.X509KeyPair (Tested above).
  2. Keep the encrypted file and decrypt at start-up with youmark/pkcs8, the passphrase coming from Secrets Manager (Tested above).
  3. Move the key into KMS or an HSM behind a crypto.Signer (case I).

golang.org/x/crypto/pkcs12 is frozen; its own docs point to software.sslmate.com/src/go-pkcs12 (Documented).

What changes in the store. Nothing. Keep the same files, formats, passwords, key types and chains. The only change is the build: Go 1.26+ toolchain and go 1.26 in go.mod, or GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 while the go line can't move.

Exact code or config change, per setup. Your loading code stays as it is. The one rule: the tls.Config it fills must not set CurvePreferences (or must include tls.X25519MLKEM768) and must not set MaxVersion: tls.VersionTLS12. The excerpts below are the tested loaders (full code in cases/main.go and deps/main.go):

// PEM pair, RSA or EC: unchanged
cert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("/etc/tls/tls.crt", "/etc/tls/tls.key")
cfg := &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}} // no CurvePreferences, no MaxVersion

// Paths from env vars (TLS_CERT_FILE / TLS_KEY_FILE): unchanged
cert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair(os.Getenv("TLS_CERT_FILE"), os.Getenv("TLS_KEY_FILE"))

// PEM content injected as env vars (ECS `secrets`, Lambda env from Secrets Manager): unchanged
cert, err := tls.X509KeyPair([]byte(os.Getenv("TLS_CERT_PEM")), []byte(os.Getenv("TLS_KEY_PEM")))

// RSA + EC on one listener: order decides which cert default clients get (first supported wins)
cfg := &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{ecCert, rsaCert}} // EC first = EC to modern clients

// Several hostnames: either a list matched by SNI ...
cfg := &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{aCert, bCert}}
// ... or a callback (hot reload, many tenants)
cfg := &tls.Config{GetCertificate: func(h *tls.ClientHelloInfo) (*tls.Certificate, error) {
    if c, ok := byName[h.ServerName]; ok { return c, nil }
    return &defaultCert, nil
}}

// PKCS#12 / PFX (OpenSSL 3 default or legacy): software.sslmate.com/src/go-pkcs12
key, leaf, chain, err := pkcs12.DecodeChain(p12Bytes, os.Getenv("TLS_KEY_PASS"))
c := tls.Certificate{PrivateKey: key, Leaf: leaf, Certificate: [][]byte{leaf.Raw}}
for _, ca := range chain { c.Certificate = append(c.Certificate, ca.Raw) }

// Encrypted PKCS#8 ("BEGIN ENCRYPTED PRIVATE KEY"): github.com/youmark/pkcs8
blk, _ := pem.Decode(keyPEM)
key, err := pkcs8.ParsePKCS8PrivateKey(blk.Bytes, []byte(os.Getenv("TLS_KEY_PASS")))

// Legacy encrypted PEM ("Proc-Type: 4,ENCRYPTED"): stdlib, deprecated; migrate when you can
blk, _ := pem.Decode(keyPEM)
der, err := x509.DecryptPEMBlock(blk, []byte(pass)) //nolint:staticcheck
cert, err := tls.X509KeyPair(certPEM, pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: blk.Type, Bytes: der}))

If you load PKCS#12 with golang.org/x/crypto/pkcs12, switch the import to software.sslmate.com/src/go-pkcs12 when your files come from OpenSSL 3 (its default PKCS#12 format). Or re-export them with openssl pkcs12 -export -keypbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -certpbe PBE-SHA1-3DES -macalg sha1. Prefer the import change, because the legacy format uses 3DES and SHA-1.

Tested proof. Go 1.26.11 server, OpenSSL 3.5.7 s_client -brief -CAfile ca.pem -verify_return_error, from run-v2.out. The server log is Go's own ConnectionState().CurveID:

port=9443 case="C rsa LoadX509KeyPair" TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
port=9444 case="C ec LoadX509KeyPair" TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
probe C two certs [rsa,ec] -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 | OK | Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768 | cert=CN=srv-rsa
probe C two certs [rsa,ec] ... -sigalgs ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 | OK | X25519MLKEM768 | cert=CN=srv-ec
probe C two certs [ec,rsa] -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 | OK | X25519MLKEM768 | cert=CN=srv-ec
port=9447 case="C SNI Certificates=[a.test,b.test]" group=X25519MLKEM768 sni="a.test"   (cert=CN=a.test)
port=9447 ... group=X25519 sni="b.test"   (classical client, cert=CN=b.test)
port=9448 case="C GetCertificate by SNI" group=X25519MLKEM768 sni="c.test"   (fallback cert=CN=srv-ec)
port=9449 case="C encrypted legacy PEM key" TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
port=9455 case="C cert+key PEM from env vars" TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
port=9460 case="C PKCS#12 modern via sslmate DecodeChain" group=X25519MLKEM768 leaf=srv-ec
port=9461 case="C PKCS#12 legacy via x/crypto Decode" group=X25519MLKEM768 leaf=srv-rsa
port=9462 case="C encrypted PKCS#8 via youmark/pkcs8" group=X25519MLKEM768 leaf=srv-ec
case="C x/crypto Decode on modern PKCS#12" load_error=pkcs12: unknown digest algorithm: 2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.1

Each server also served X25519 to a classical client (fallback). Go 1.24.13 (go 1.24) and 1.25.14 gave the same OK results. Go 1.23.12 and 1.24.13 with go 1.22 failed every PQ-only probe with the same stores. The test files were made by gen-certs.sh: RSA 2048, EC P-256, and the PKCS#12 formats confirmed with openssl pkcs12 -info: AES-256-CBC/PBKDF2/SHA-256 MAC, and 3DES/SHA-1.

Side effects. None for PQ. If you list RSA before EC, default clients get RSA; that was already true.

D. Custom CA trust

Who this is. grep -rnE 'SystemCertPool|AppendCertsFromPEM|RootCAs|SSL_CERT_FILE|SSL_CERT_DIR|AWS_CA_BUNDLE|WithCustomCABundle|sslrootcert' in code and deployment files.

What happens today. Trust and key exchange are independent. Each row reached the PQ-only server with X25519MLKEM768 and the classical server with X25519, on Go 1.24.13 (go 1.24), 1.25.14 and 1.26.11 (Tested):

Trust setup Result
SSL_CERT_FILE=/certs/ca.pem, RootCAs nil PQ and fallback OK
SSL_CERT_DIR=/certs/cadir, RootCAs nil PQ and fallback OK
Neither set, private CA not in the system store x509: certificate signed by unknown authority (expected)
x509.SystemCertPool() + AppendCertsFromPEM PQ and fallback OK
RootCAs = new pool with only the private CA PQ and fallback OK
RootCAs = empty pool Unknown authority (expected)
AWS SDK AWS_CA_BUNDLE or config.WithCustomCABundle, default HTTP client PQ OK (1.26.11)
AWS SDK CA bundle + a plain *http.Client Config error: unable to add custom RootCAs HTTPClient, has no WithTransportOptions, *http.Client (1.26.11)
gRPC credentials.NewClientTLSFromFile(ca.pem, ...) PQ OK (1.26.11)
pgx DSN sslrootcert= PQ OK (1.26.11)

SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR replace the default locations, they don't add to them (Documented). Put public roots in that file too if the service also calls public endpoints.

What changes in the truststore. Nothing. Keep the same CA bundle files, directories, env vars and pools. Rebuild with Go 1.26+ and go 1.26, or set GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 in the interim.

Exact code or config change, per setup. Your trust code stays as it is, with one exception (the AWS row). The tested forms:

// 1. Env-var trust (no code): SSL_CERT_FILE or SSL_CERT_DIR, RootCAs left nil
//    Dockerfile:   ENV SSL_CERT_FILE=/etc/ssl/certs/bundle-with-private-ca.pem
//    ECS taskdef:  "environment": [{"name": "SSL_CERT_FILE", "value": "/etc/ssl/certs/bundle-with-private-ca.pem"}]
//    Lambda / systemd: same variable. It REPLACES the default file, so the bundle must also hold public roots
//    if the service calls public endpoints.
cfg := &tls.Config{} // RootCAs nil = system pool built from SSL_CERT_FILE / SSL_CERT_DIR

// 2. System roots plus your private CA
pool, err := x509.SystemCertPool()
if err != nil { pool = x509.NewCertPool() }
pool.AppendCertsFromPEM(caPEM)
cfg := &tls.Config{RootCAs: pool}

// 3. Private CA only (internal endpoints)
pool := x509.NewCertPool(); pool.AppendCertsFromPEM(caPEM)
cfg := &tls.Config{RootCAs: pool}

// 4. AWS SDK: AWS_CA_BUNDLE env or WithCustomCABundle needs the SDK's BuildableClient
cfg, err := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithCustomCABundle(caFile)) // default client: works
// With your own client: do NOT pass a plain *http.Client together with a CA bundle (config error).
// Set RootCAs on a BuildableClient instead:
hc := awshttp.NewBuildableClient().WithTransportOptions(func(t *http.Transport) {
    t.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{RootCAs: pool} // no CurvePreferences
})
cfg, err := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithHTTPClient(hc))

// 5. gRPC
creds, err := credentials.NewClientTLSFromFile("/etc/ssl/private-ca.pem", "api.internal")

// 6. pgx / database/sql
//    postgres://app@db.internal:5432/app?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/rds-ca.pem

On scratch or distroless static images there is no system bundle. Copy one in (COPY --from=build /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt /etc/ssl/certs/) or use form 3.

Tested proof. Go client against the OpenSSL 3.5.7 PQ-only server (:8443) and the classical server (:8444). Both use a cert issued by the private test CA. From run-v2.out, Go 1.26.11:

D | default RootCAs (SSL_CERT_FILE)            | localhost:8443 | OK   | TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
D | default RootCAs (SSL_CERT_FILE)            | localhost:8444 | OK   | TLS1.3 group=X25519
D | default RootCAs (SSL_CERT_DIR)             | localhost:8443 | OK   | TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
D | default RootCAs (no env, negative)         | localhost:8443 | FAIL | x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
D | SystemCertPool()+AppendCertsFromPEM(ca)    | localhost:8443 | OK   | TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
D | RootCAs = NewCertPool with private CA only | localhost:8443 | OK   | TLS1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768
D | RootCAs = empty pool (negative)            | localhost:8443 | FAIL | x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
H | aws-sdk | default client + AWS_CA_BUNDLE env           | :8443 | TLS-OK (then protocol error: test server isn't STS)
H | aws-sdk | default client + WithCustomCABundle          | :8443 | TLS-OK
H | aws-sdk | plain *http.Client + WithCustomCABundle      | :8443 | config: unable to add custom RootCAs HTTPClient, has no WithTransportOptions, *http.Client
H | grpc    | credentials.NewClientTLSFromFile(ca.pem)     | :9473 | TLS-OK   (observer: X25519MLKEM768)
H | pgx     | DSN sslrootcert+sslcert+sslkey               | :9471 | observer=raw group=X25519MLKEM768 client_cn=cli-ec

The 8443 server accepts only X25519MLKEM768, so every OK against it proves PQ. Go 1.24.13 (go 1.24) and 1.25.14 gave the same results. Go 1.23.12 and 1.24.13 with go 1.22 failed on 8443 with every trust setup and passed on 8444. So trust was never the cause.

Side effects. None.

E. Mutual TLS (client certificates)

Who this is. grep -rnE --include='*.go' 'ClientAuth|ClientCAs|GetClientCertificate|Certificates:' .

What happens today. Client certificates don't change the group (Tested on 1.24.13 go 1.24, 1.25.14, 1.26.11):

  • Go client with Certificates: {RSA client cert} or GetClientCertificate returning an EC cert, against an OpenSSL server with -Verify 1: X25519MLKEM768 when PQ-only, X25519 when classical-only.
  • Go server with ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert and ClientCAs: RSA and EC clients over X25519MLKEM768, client_cn logged; a classical client over X25519.
  • No client cert: refused as expected. In TLS 1.3 the client sees the error on its first read (remote error: tls: certificate required); the server logs tls: client didn't provide a certificate.
  • AWS SDK, gRPC and pgx with a client cert: case H.

What to change. Nothing. Side effects. None.

F. Explicit TLS settings that block PQ

Who this is. Run go-pq-lint.sh (Full configuration files), or:

grep -rnE --include='*.go' 'CurvePreferences|MaxVersion|CipherSuites|tlsmlkem|tlskyber|fipsonly' . $(go env GOMODCACHE) | grep -v _test.go
grep -rnE 'GODEBUG|godebug' go.mod go.work Dockerfile* *.yaml *.json *.tf 2>/dev/null

What happens today (client: Go vs OpenSSL servers; server: Go vs OpenSSL s_client; Go 1.24.13 go 1.24, 1.25.14, 1.26.11; all Tested):

Setting Client to PQ-only server Client to classical As a server Change to
CurvePreferences: {X25519, P256} Fails: handshake failure X25519 PQ-only client fails; a hybrid-capable client silently gets X25519 Remove it, or add tls.X25519MLKEM768 (and tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768 on 1.26+)
CurvePreferences: {X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P256} X25519MLKEM768 X25519 — Fine. With tlsmlkem=0 (old go line) the hybrid is dropped even from this list on 1.24 to 1.26
MaxVersion: tls.VersionTLS12 Fails: protocol version not supported TLS 1.2, X25519 TLS 1.2 only, never PQ Remove it: the hybrids exist only in TLS 1.3
MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13 X25519MLKEM768 X25519 — Fine
CipherSuites (a TLS 1.2 list) X25519MLKEM768 X25519 PQ on TLS 1.3; TLS 1.2 clients limited to the list Keep: it doesn't touch TLS 1.3
GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0 at run time Fails X25519 — Remove it
GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1 on a go 1.22 module X25519MLKEM768 X25519 PQ too Interim fix until the go line moves
Go 1.23 with curve 4588 listed by number Fails even to classical: tls: CurvePreferences includes unsupported curve Fails — Upgrade the toolchain

PQ-only enforcement (internal endpoints, after all clients are PQ):

cfg := &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS13,
    CurvePreferences: []tls.CurveID{tls.X25519MLKEM768, tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768}}

Side effects. Removing MaxVersion lets TLS 1.3 through; check peers that pin TLS 1.2 behaviour, such as inspection proxies.

G. FIPS mode

Who this is. go version -m shows GOFIPS140=, fips140=on or GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto, or the environment sets GODEBUG=fips140=on|only.

What happens today. See the table: Go 1.24 FIPS and boringcrypto fipsonly give no PQ; Go 1.26+ native FIPS offers all three hybrids. The AWS SDK forces classical curves in FIPS mode (case H).

What to change. Build with Go 1.26+ and GOFIPS140=v1.26.0 or latest; add the AWS SDK fix.

FIPS 140-3 mode (GOFIPS140=latest|v1.0.0|v1.26.0 at build, or GODEBUG=fips140=on). crypto/tls silently drops non-approved groups (Documented). Client results (groups offered; a server that prefers P-256 negotiates P-256. Tested: e2e go-*-fips*, Lambda, Fargate and EC2):

Mode 1.24.13 1.25.14 1.26.11 1.27.4
fips140=on P-256, P-384, P-521 only: no PQ, no X25519 X25519MLKEM768, P-256, P-384, P-521 X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024, P-256, P-384, P-521 Same as 1.26
fips140=only P-256, P-384, P-521 only Every handshake fails: crypto/ecdh: use of X25519 is not allowed in FIPS 140-only mode Same as on Same as on
GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto, no fipsonly Same as non-FIPS (PQ yes) Same as non-FIPS Same as non-FIPS Same as non-FIPS
boringcrypto + import _ "crypto/tls/fipsonly" not run P-256, P-384, P-521 only, no PQ Same Same
boringcrypto + fips140=on Panics at start: FIPS 140-3 mode is incompatible with GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto Same Same Same

All cells Tested. In FIPS mode a server that offers only X25519 can't be reached, whatever the PQ setting. The TLS group policy follows the toolchain, not the module version: GOFIPS140=v1.0.0 built with 1.26 offered the SecP hybrids (Tested). Module v1.0.0 holds CMVP certificate #5247; v1.26.0 is in process (Go FIPS page, as of 2026-04-28).

H. Libraries with their own TLS settings

Who this is. You pass a tls.Config to the AWS SDK, gRPC or a database driver, often to add a private CA or a client certificate.

What happens today. All three pass your tls.Config through unchanged, PQ included. Tested with Go 1.26.11, a custom config holding the private CA in RootCAs and an EC client cert, against a Go observer server (PQ-only, mTLS required, logs the group and client CN), an OpenSSL PQ-only mTLS server and an OpenSSL classical mTLS server:

Library How the config was passed Observer OpenSSL PQ-only Classical Same config + CurvePreferences {X25519, P256} Run with GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0
aws-sdk-go-v2 v1.48.0, config v1.33.18 awshttp.NewBuildableClient().WithTransportOptions(t.TLSClientConfig = cfg) X25519MLKEM768, client_cn=cli-ec OK OK Fails to PQ-only: config passed through Fails to PQ-only
same plain &http.Client{Transport: &http.Transport{TLSClientConfig: cfg}} via config.WithHTTPClient X25519MLKEM768, cli-ec OK OK — Fails to PQ-only
grpc-go v1.85.0 credentials.NewTLS(cfg) X25519MLKEM768, cli-ec — — Fails Fails
grpc-go v1.85.0 credentials.NewClientTLSFromFile(ca.pem, name) X25519MLKEM768 (no mTLS) — — — Fails
pgx v5.13.0 ConnConfig.TLSConfig = cfg, sslnegotiation=direct X25519MLKEM768, cli-ec OK OK Fails Fails
pgx v5.13.0 DSN sslrootcert, sslcert, sslkey X25519MLKEM768, cli-ec OK OK — Fails

pgx was tested only with direct TLS; the default sslnegotiation=postgres (TLS after SSLRequest) uses the same tls.Config but was not run (Unverified). The FIPS-mode curve override in the AWS SDK is the one library default that blocks PQ.

Outside Go's TLS: confluent-kafka-go uses librdkafka with its own OpenSSL, and anything you exec (curl, git, wget) uses the image's TLS library. Debian and Ubuntu GnuTLS has no ML-KEM (lead's test, Java tab notes). Neither was tested from Go (Unverified).

gRPC-go. credentials.NewTLS keeps your tls.Config as given. Avoid helpers that build a config with a fixed curve list.

creds := credentials.NewTLS(&tls.Config{ServerName: "api.internal"})
conn, err := grpc.NewClient("api.internal:443", grpc.WithTransportCredentials(creds))

AWS SDK for Go v2. Outside FIPS mode the default HTTP client leaves CurvePreferences nil, so it offers X25519MLKEM768 (Tested). In FIPS mode (GOFIPS140 build or GODEBUG=fips140=on), v1.48.0's aws/transport/http/client.go sets CurvePreferences to P-256, P-384 and P-521. The handshake to a PQ-only server then failed (Tested). I'm not sure which SDK release added this. Put the FIPS-approved hybrids back (Tested: PQ-only server then succeeded):

hc := awshttp.NewBuildableClient().WithTransportOptions(func(t *http.Transport) {
    if fips140.Enabled() {
        t.TLSClientConfig.CurvePreferences = []tls.CurveID{
            tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768, tls.X25519MLKEM768, tls.CurveP256, tls.CurveP384}
    }
})
cfg, _ := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithHTTPClient(hc))

pgx, database/sql. sslmode=verify-full builds a tls.Config without curves. Your own ConnConfig.TLSConfig must not add any.

pc, _ := pgx.ParseConfig("postgres://app@db.internal:5432/app?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/rds-ca.pem")
conn, err := pgx.ConnectConfig(ctx, pc)

go-redis, kafka-go, sarama.

rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{Addr: "cache.internal:6379", TLSConfig: &tls.Config{ServerName: "cache.internal"}})
dialer := &kafka.Dialer{TLS: &tls.Config{}}               // kafka-go
sc := sarama.NewConfig(); sc.Net.TLS.Enable = true; sc.Net.TLS.Config = &tls.Config{} // sarama

I. Pinning, and HSM, PKCS#11 or KMS keys

Who this is. VerifyPeerCertificate or VerifyConnection with SPKI hashes; a tls.Certificate whose PrivateKey is a KMS, CloudHSM or PKCS#11 crypto.Signer.

What happens today.

  • SPKI pinning in VerifyConnection: the right pin passed over X25519MLKEM768 and over X25519; a wrong pin failed with your error (Tested 1.24.13, 1.26.11). PQ key exchange doesn't change certificates, so pins stay valid. They change only when you move to ML-DSA certificates.
  • A server key behind an opaque crypto.Signer (only Public and Sign, the shape KMS and PKCS#11 wrappers expose), RSA and EC: Sign was called once per handshake and X25519MLKEM768 was negotiated (Tested 1.24.13, 1.26.11). The ML-KEM part runs in software in crypto/tls; the HSM only signs. A real KMS, CloudHSM or PKCS#11 module was not tested (no AWS access).

What to change. Nothing. Side effects. None.

J. Other cases

  • Behind a load balancer. The front door may own the client-facing handshake (table below).
  • HTTPS_PROXY. net/http tunnels TLS through CONNECT, so the Go client's settings still decide, unless the proxy intercepts TLS; then the proxy's stack decides (Unverified; see Network devices and egress).
  • HTTP/2 and gRPC servers. ALPN h2 and X25519MLKEM768 work together (Tested, earlier pass).
  • WebSockets (gorilla/websocket, coder/websocket) dial through net/http or a tls.Config; same rules (Unverified).
  • Service mesh sidecar. If the app talks plaintext to the sidecar, the mesh decides (see Service mesh).

Behind a load balancer.

Front Who decides the client-facing handshake Go server's part
ALB (HTTPS listener) The ALB security policy Only the ALB-to-target leg. With a PQ listener policy the ALB uses ELBSecurityPolicy-TLS13-1-0-PQ-2025-09 towards HTTPS targets (Documented), so a PQ-capable Go target negotiates ML-KEM on that leg.
NLB, TCP listener (passthrough) Your Go server Everything above applies
NLB, TLS listener The NLB security policy Only the NLB-to-target leg
API Gateway, CloudFront The front door Origin legs are classical

See Load balancers, Edge and API front doors and Web servers and proxies for those policies.

Solution and automation

  1. Inventory. Run go-pq-posture.sh over every built artifact (Lambda bootstrap, files copied out of images, EC2 binaries) and go-pq-lint.sh over every repo. Export GODEBUG from Lambda configurations, task definitions and pod specs. Use CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange for KMS, STS, IAM, Secrets Manager and ACM callers.
  2. Change. Raise the go line to 1.26 and rebuild with Go 1.26+. Remove blocking settings (case F). For FIPS, move to native GOFIPS140 and apply the AWS SDK fix (cases G, H). Where the go line can't move yet, set GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=1,tlssecpmlkem=1. Packaging per compute type is below.
  3. CI guardrails. Fail the build on go-pq-lint.sh findings before compiling, then run go-pq-posture.sh on the built binary. Both scripts are in Full configuration files. The lint is a file-level heuristic: a file that mentions ML-KEM anywhere passes its CurvePreferences check, so review hits by hand.
  4. Fleet rollout. Clients first: they fall back to X25519, so a client change can't break a classical server. Then servers, which still accept classical clients. PQ-only enforcement comes last, per endpoint, after the logs show no classical clients. Canary one function version, one task set or one Deployment, and watch tls_group= logs, handshake errors and p99 latency for a day. Roll back with GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0,tlssecpmlkem=0 in the environment (no rebuild).

Packaging per compute type

Every compute type takes the same two levers: rebuild with Go 1.26+ and go 1.26+ (preferred), or set GODEBUG in the deployment config when the go line can't move yet. Full files are in the last section.

Lambda zip (provided.al2023). The binary must be named bootstrap at the zip root (AWS).

GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -tags lambda.norpc -o bootstrap .
zip function.zip bootstrap
go version -m bootstrap | grep -E '^bootstrap|DefaultGODEBUG'   # posture before deploy

SAM: Metadata: BuildMethod: go1.x, Runtime: provided.al2023, Handler: bootstrap. If needed: Environment.Variables.GODEBUG: tlsmlkem=1,tlssecpmlkem=1. CloudFormation and Terraform set the same variable.

Lambda container image. Multi-stage build: golang:1.26 builder, public.ecr.aws/lambda/provided:al2023 final stage (AWS). Set GODEBUG with ENV in the Dockerfile or in the function's environment.

Fargate, ECS, EKS. Build on golang:1.26, ship on gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot or scratch (copy CA certificates). An optional GODEBUG goes in the task definition environment or the pod env.

EC2. Ship the binary. An optional Environment=GODEBUG=... goes in the systemd unit, rolled out with SSM Run Command or your AMI pipeline.

FIPS builds. GOFIPS140=v1.26.0 (or latest) at build time; go version -m shows GOFIPS140= and DefaultGODEBUG=fips140=on.

How to test

  1. Posture. Run go version -m on the artifact (table below).
  2. Code scan. Run go-pq-lint.sh .; it must print go-pq-lint: OK.
  3. Local harness. Run gen-certs.sh and pq-servers.sh in debian:trixie-slim (OpenSSL 3.5). They start a PQ-only server on 8443, a classical-only server on 8444, and mTLS versions of both on 8445 and 8446. Run your client against each. It must reach 8443 (PQ) and 8444 (fallback).
  4. Case C (your server and its store). Start your server with its real cert files or keystore and run: openssl s_client -brief -connect host:port -CAfile ca.pem -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 → Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768; -groups X25519 → still connects. For several certificates add -servername <each name>, and -sigalgs ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 or -sigalgs rsa_pss_rsae_sha256:rsa_pkcs1_sha256 to see each one. For a TLS 1.2 probe of an ECDSA P-256 cert, offer -groups X25519:P-256; with X25519 alone OpenSSL fails with wrong curve, which is a probe artifact.
  5. Case D. Point the client at 8443 with your CA setup (SSL_CERT_FILE, your pool, AWS_CA_BUNDLE); then with no CA, which must fail with unknown authority.
  6. Case E. Client with its cert against 8445 must succeed; without it, it must fail with certificate required. Your mTLS server: s_client ... -cert client.pem -key client.key must succeed, and the server log must show client_cn.
  7. In-cloud signal. Server tls_group= logs and CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange (below).
  8. Rollback test. Restart with GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0: 8443 must now fail and 8444 still work. Remove it, and 8443 works again.

The cases program (cases/main.go) and the library program (deps/main.go) used for this tab are in Full configuration files; outputs are in run-v2.out, run-v2b.out and run-v2c.out.

Details for the steps

Posture, without running anything. go version -m reads the build info from any Go binary: Lambda bootstrap, a file copied out of an image, or a binary on an EC2 host (Tested).

$ go version -m probe-go1.26-mod1.23
probe-go1.26-mod1.23: go1.26.11
        build   DefaultGODEBUG=...,tlsmlkem=0,tlssecpmlkem=0,...
$ go version -m probe-go1.26-mod1.26
probe-go1.26-mod1.26: go1.26.11            # no DefaultGODEBUG line = toolchain defaults = PQ
go version -m shows Meaning
go1.23.x or older No PQ possible: rebuild
tlsmlkem=0 in DefaultGODEBUG Classical: raise the go line or set tlsmlkem=1
tlssecpmlkem=0 X25519MLKEM768 only, no SecP hybrids (matters for FIPS)
GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto Check for crypto/tls/fipsonly (no PQ with it)
GOFIPS140= / fips140=on FIPS mode: needs Go 1.25+ for any PQ, 1.26+ for the SecP hybrids

Runtime GODEBUG env vars aren't in the binary, so also check the function, task or pod environment. The go-pq-posture.sh script in the last section checks every binary in a folder and fails CI.

Code scan. CurvePreferences anywhere in your code or dependencies disables the defaults.

grep -rn --include='*.go' 'CurvePreferences' . $(go env GOMODCACHE) | grep -v _test.go

In the tested versions, only the AWS SDK hit (its FIPS list).

Live test. Run two servers from an OpenSSL 3.5 image. The client must reach both: the PQ-only one proves PQ, the classical one proves fallback.

openssl s_server -accept 8443 -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -www   # PQ-only
openssl s_server -accept 8444 -groups X25519 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -www                   # classical-only

For a Go server, run both of these:

  • openssl s_client -connect host:443 -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 must print Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768.

  • -groups X25519 must still connect, unless PQ-only is the goal.

Observed signal. Server logs tls_group= (see below). For AWS calls, check CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange = X25519MLKEM768 (KMS, STS, IAM, Secrets Manager, ACM only; see AWS service endpoints).

Observed signal. Go 1.25+ exposes the group: log r.TLS.CurveID in HTTP handlers and credentials.TLSInfo.State.CurveID in a gRPC interceptor. Lines from the test server:

grpc addr=:9446 tls_group=X25519MLKEM768
raw addr=:9449 handshake_error=tls: no key exchanges supported by both client and server

Pitfalls and rollback

  • New toolchain, old go line. The most common miss: Go 1.27 with go 1.23 stayed classical (Tested). Check DefaultGODEBUG, not the toolchain.

  • CurvePreferences set anywhere. One explicit list without a hybrid makes that client or server classical, and the fallback is silent (Tested). Check libraries too (AWS SDK in FIPS mode).

  • FIPS on Go 1.24 or boringcrypto + fipsonly. No PQ at all (Tested). Go 1.25 with fips140=only fails every handshake (Tested).

  • Go 1.26 with go 1.25. X25519MLKEM768 works but SecP256r1MLKEM768 doesn't. That is the only hybrid FIPS-oriented servers may accept.

  • Big ClientHello. ML-KEM adds about 1.2 KB, so the ClientHello spans two TCP segments. Broken middleboxes time out (tldr.fail). See Network devices and egress.

  • tlsmlkem=0 beats your explicit list on 1.24 to 1.26. Don't leave it set "temporarily".

  • RSA listed before EC. With Certificates: {rsa, ec} default clients get RSA. Not a PQ issue, but surprising during cert migrations (Tested).

  • x/crypto/pkcs12 can't read OpenSSL 3 default PKCS#12 files. It fails at start-up with unknown digest algorithm; use go-pkcs12 (Tested).

  • AWS CA bundle with your own *http.Client. AWS_CA_BUNDLE or WithCustomCABundle then fails at config load (Tested).

  • Go 1.23 isn't "almost PQ". Its Kyber draft group (0x6399) isn't ML-KEM; standard PQ-only servers refuse it (Tested).

  • mTLS errors move to the first read in TLS 1.3. A missing client cert shows up as certificate required on read, not on dial (Tested).

Rollback, fastest first. No code change is needed.

  1. Set GODEBUG=tlsmlkem=0,tlssecpmlkem=0 in the function, task or pod environment, then redeploy or restart.

  2. Rebuild with godebug tlsmlkem=0 in go.mod.

  3. Redeploy the previous artifact.

Remove the override once the peer is fixed, and record it as a temporary exception with an owner and an end date.

Full configuration files

These files match the excerpts above. Replace the example account IDs, names and ARNs with your own. The Go sources compile against Go 1.26. Tested parts are marked in the sections above; IaC files follow AWS docs and were not deployed (no AWS access here).

    github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config v1.33.18

Versions are what go mod tidy resolved on 2026-11-14 (the sources in this section compile and pass go vet with Go 1.26.11). Only the go line matters for PQ.

go.mod (alternative: keep an old go line, turn PQ on)

module example.com/legacy

go 1.23

godebug (
    tlsmlkem=1
    tlssecpmlkem=1
)

tlssecpmlkem is only known to Go 1.26+ toolchains. On 1.24 or 1.25 builds, list tlsmlkem=1 only, or the build fails on an unknown setting.

cmd/client/main.go (HTTP and AWS SDK client, FIPS-safe)

//go:debug tlsmlkem=1
package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/fips140"
    "crypto/tls"
    "log"
    "net/http"
    "time"

    awshttp "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/aws/transport/http"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/config"
    "github.com/aws/aws-sdk-go-v2/service/sts"
)

// The //go:debug line is optional: needed only while go.mod says go < 1.24.

func httpClient() *http.Client {
    tr := http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport).Clone()
    tr.TLSClientConfig = &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12} // no CurvePreferences
    return &http.Client{Transport: tr, Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
}

func awsHTTPClient() *awshttp.BuildableClient {
    return awshttp.NewBuildableClient().WithTransportOptions(func(t *http.Transport) {
        if fips140.Enabled() {
            // aws-sdk-go-v2 v1.48.0 forces P-256/384/521 in FIPS mode; keep the approved hybrids.
            t.TLSClientConfig.CurvePreferences = []tls.CurveID{
                tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768, tls.X25519MLKEM768, tls.CurveP256, tls.CurveP384}
        }
    })
}

func main() {
    ctx := context.Background()
    cfg, err := config.LoadDefaultConfig(ctx, config.WithHTTPClient(awsHTTPClient()))
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    out, err := sts.NewFromConfig(cfg).GetCallerIdentity(ctx, &sts.GetCallerIdentityInput{})
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    log.Printf("caller=%s", *out.Arn)

    resp, err := httpClient().Get("https://api.internal.example.com/health")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    log.Printf("status=%d tls_group=%v", resp.StatusCode, resp.TLS.CurveID)
}

cmd/server/main.go (HTTPS and gRPC server that logs the group)

package main

import (
    "context"
    "crypto/tls"
    "log"
    "net"
    "net/http"
    "os"

    "google.golang.org/grpc"
    "google.golang.org/grpc/credentials"
    "google.golang.org/grpc/health"
    healthpb "google.golang.org/grpc/health/grpc_health_v1"
    "google.golang.org/grpc/peer"
)

func tlsConfig() *tls.Config {
    cert, err := tls.LoadX509KeyPair("/etc/tls/tls.crt", "/etc/tls/tls.key")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    cfg := &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}, MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12}
    if os.Getenv("TLS_PQ_ONLY") == "1" { // enforcement mode, after every client is PQ
        cfg.MinVersion = tls.VersionTLS13
        cfg.CurvePreferences = []tls.CurveID{tls.X25519MLKEM768, tls.SecP256r1MLKEM768}
    }
    return cfg
}

func main() {
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("/", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        log.Printf("path=%s tls_version=%x tls_group=%v", r.URL.Path, r.TLS.Version, r.TLS.CurveID)
        w.Write([]byte("ok\n"))
    })
    go func() {
        srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8443", Handler: mux, TLSConfig: tlsConfig()}
        log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS("", ""))
    }()

    lis, err := net.Listen("tcp", ":9443")
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    gs := grpc.NewServer(grpc.Creds(credentials.NewTLS(tlsConfig())),
        grpc.UnaryInterceptor(func(ctx context.Context, req any, info *grpc.UnaryServerInfo, h grpc.UnaryHandler) (any, error) {
            if p, ok := peer.FromContext(ctx); ok {
                if ti, ok := p.AuthInfo.(credentials.TLSInfo); ok {
                    log.Printf("grpc method=%s tls_group=%v", info.FullMethod, ti.State.CurveID)
                }
            }
            return h(ctx, req)
        }))
    healthpb.RegisterHealthServer(gs, health.NewServer())
    log.Fatal(gs.Serve(lis))
}
