fortigate-ipsec-pq.conf (FortiOS 7.6.5+ CLI. The addke1 and childless-ike lines are from the Fortinet guide; interface, proposal and peer lines are placeholders. Not tested)

# addke IDs: 35 = ML-KEM-512, 36 = ML-KEM-768, 37 = ML-KEM-1024 (not available in FIPS-CC mode)
config vpn ipsec phase1-interface
    edit "to-aws-pq"
        set interface "port1"
        set ike-version 2
        set peertype any
        set net-device disable
        set proposal aes256gcm-prfsha384
        set dhgrp 20
        set addke1 36
        set childless-ike enable
        set fragmentation enable
        set remote-gw 203.0.113.10
        set psksecret <psk>
    next
end
config vpn ipsec phase2-interface
    edit "to-aws-pq-p2"
        set phase1name "to-aws-pq"
        set proposal aes256gcm
        set dhgrp 20
        set addke1 36
    next
end
# Verify:  diagnose vpn ike gateway list name to-aws-pq  ->  PQC-KEM (IKE): yes / PQC-KEM (all IPsec): yes

f5-pq.tmsh (BIG-IP 17.5.1+, TLS 1.3 only. Steps 1–3 are from the F5 guide; the server-ssl line is our inference from the documented GUI step)

# 1. Cipher rule: hybrid first, then the default groups (classical fallback)
create ltm cipher rule PQ_HYBRID cipher DEFAULT dh-groups X25519MLKEM768:DEFAULT signature-algorithms DEFAULT
# 2. Cipher group that allows the rule
create ltm cipher group PQ_HYBRID allow add { PQ_HYBRID }
# 3. Client leg (clients -> virtual server)
create ltm profile client-ssl clientssl-pq defaults-from clientssl cipher-group PQ_HYBRID ciphers none options { dont-insert-empty-fragments }
# 4. Server leg (BIG-IP -> pool); GUI: Server SSL profile > Cipher Group
create ltm profile server-ssl serverssl-pq defaults-from serverssl cipher-group PQ_HYBRID ciphers none
# 5. Attach to the virtual server
modify ltm virtual vs_app_443 profiles add { clientssl-pq { context clientside } serverssl-pq { context serverside } }
save sys config

netscaler-pq.cli (NetScaler 14.1, front end only. Only the bind ssl profile … -eccCurveName lines are from the NetScaler page; check the profile setup lines against your build)

set ssl parameter -defaultProfile ENABLED
add ssl profile fe_pq -sslProfileType FrontEnd -tls13 ENABLED
# Either append the hybrid group to the bound curves ...
bind ssl profile fe_pq -eccCurveName X25519_MLKEM768
# ... or rebind ALL (puts X25519_MLKEM768 first):  bind ssl profile fe_pq -eccCurveName ALL
set ssl vserver vs_app_443 -sslProfile fe_pq
# GUI: Traffic Management > SSL > SSL Profiles > fe_pq > Advanced Settings > ECC Curve > X25519_MLKEM768 > Bind

/etc/openvpn/server/pq.conf (PQ lines) (OpenVPN 2.6 linked to OpenSSL 3.5+ on both ends; Documented in the 2.6 manual and the vendor tutorial; add to your existing server and client configs)

tls-version-min 1.3
# Prefer hybrid, keep classical for peers without OpenSSL 3.5 (drop ":X25519" to require PQ)
tls-groups X25519MLKEM768:X25519
# Log line to check: "key agreement: X25519MLKEM768"

/opt/zeek/share/zeek/site/pq-tls.zeek (Tested, Zeek 8.0.10; add @load ./pq-tls to local.zeek)

##! pq-tls.zeek - flag TLS sessions whose negotiated key exchange is not hybrid post-quantum.
##! Needs Zeek 7.1+ (SSL::ec_curves knows 0x11EC = X25519MLKEM768).
@load base/protocols/ssl
@load base/frameworks/notice

module PQTLS;

export {
    redef enum Notice::Type += { PQTLS::Classical_Key_Exchange };

    ## Groups counted as post-quantum (hybrid ML-KEM).
    const pq_groups: set[string] = {
        "X25519MLKEM768", "SecP256r1MLKEM768", "SecP384r1MLKEM1024",
    } &redef;

    ## Add a boolean column "pq" to ssl.log.
    redef record SSL::Info += {
        pq: bool &log &optional;
    };
}

event ssl_established(c: connection) &priority=3
    {
    if ( ! c?$ssl ) return;
    local grp = c$ssl?$curve ? c$ssl$curve : "none";
    c$ssl$pq = grp in pq_groups;
    if ( ! c$ssl$pq )
        NOTICE([$note=PQTLS::Classical_Key_Exchange,
                $msg=fmt("non-PQ TLS key exchange: group=%s version=%s sni=%s", grp,
                         c$ssl?$version ? c$ssl$version : "?",
                         c$ssl?$server_name ? c$ssl$server_name : "-"),
                $conn=c,
                $identifier=cat(c$id$resp_h, c$id$resp_p, grp),
                $suppress_for=1hr]);
    }

traffic-mirror.tf (Terraform; not deployed. Mirrored packets arrive at the sensor as VXLAN on UDP 4789, so allow that in the sensor's security group)

variable "source_eni_id" { type = string } # NAT instance / proxy / app host ENI (Nitro)
variable "sensor_eni_id" { type = string } # Zeek sensor ENI

resource "aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_target" "zeek" {
  network_interface_id = var.sensor_eni_id
  description          = "Zeek PQ TLS sensor"
}

resource "aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter" "tls" {
  description = "TLS handshakes only"
}

resource "aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter_rule" "egress_443" {
  traffic_mirror_filter_id = aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter.tls.id
  traffic_direction        = "egress"
  rule_number              = 100
  rule_action              = "accept"
  protocol                 = 6
  destination_port_range {
    from_port = 443
    to_port   = 443
  }
  source_cidr_block      = "0.0.0.0/0"
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
}

resource "aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter_rule" "ingress_443" {
  traffic_mirror_filter_id = aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter.tls.id
  traffic_direction        = "ingress"
  rule_number              = 100
  rule_action              = "accept"
  protocol                 = 6
  source_port_range {
    from_port = 443
    to_port   = 443
  }
  source_cidr_block      = "0.0.0.0/0"
  destination_cidr_block = "0.0.0.0/0"
}

resource "aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_session" "src" {
  network_interface_id     = var.source_eni_id
  traffic_mirror_target_id = aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_target.zeek.id
  traffic_mirror_filter_id = aws_ec2_traffic_mirror_filter.tls.id
  session_number           = 1
  virtual_network_id       = 4242
  # No packet_length: the hybrid ClientHello spans two segments, so don't truncate.
  description = "PQ TLS sensor"
}

IoT devices

What decides PQ here

The device's TLS library decides the client side, and the broker decides the server side. On microcontrollers that library is the one compiled into the firmware: Mbed TLS (the FreeRTOS, ESP-IDF and Zephyr default) has no ML-KEM, while wolfSSL does. On Linux-class devices it is the system OpenSSL, or the s2n-tls + AWS-LC stack bundled inside the AWS CRT that the AWS IoT Device SDKs v2 use. On the server side, AWS IoT Core offers no PQ security policy, so device-to-IoT Core connections stay classical whatever the device offers. PQ is achievable today only on hops you control: a self-run broker (Mosquitto, EMQX, HiveMQ), a gateway's uplink to your own endpoints, or a PQ tunnel.

The plan therefore has three parts: ship PQ-capable stacks in new and updatable devices now, enforce PQ on brokers and gateways you run, and move IoT Core traffic when AWS adds a PQ policy. All tests on this tab ran on 2026-11-14 in local containers, without AWS access. Scripts and outputs are in the work directory deep/netiot/ (mosq/, wolf/).

Client side (devices)

Microcontrollers: wolfSSL, the only MCU path to ML-KEM today

  • Build: wolfSSL 5.9.1+ builds ML-KEM by default. For older 5.8.x builds or user_settings.h builds, define WOLFSSL_HAVE_MLKEM, WOLFSSL_SHA3, WOLFSSL_SHAKE128, WOLFSSL_SHAKE256, HAVE_CURVE25519, WOLFSSL_TLS13 and HAVE_SUPPORTED_CURVES. Drop the sizes you don't need with WOLFSSL_NO_ML_KEM_512 / WOLFSSL_NO_ML_KEM_1024. Documented (examples/configs/user_settings_pq.h). With configure, the flag is --enable-mlkem (Claimed, wolfSSL posts).

  • Code: after wolfSSL_new(), call wolfSSL_UseKeyShare(ssl, WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768) so the first ClientHello carries the hybrid share. This avoids a HelloRetryRequest. Set the order with wolfSSL_CTX_set_groups() / wolfSSL_set_groups(), and keep WOLFSSL_ECC_X25519 and WOLFSSL_ECC_SECP256R1 after the hybrid group for fallback. Constants in wolfssl/ssl.h: WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768 = 4588, WOLFSSL_SECP256R1MLKEM768 = 4587, WOLFSSL_SECP384R1MLKEM1024 = 4589. There is no WOLFSSL_X25519_ML_KEM_768.

  • FreeRTOS coreMQTT: transport_wolfSSL.c sets no groups, so the device gets the build's defaults. Add the two calls above in TLS_FreeRTOS_Connect after wolfSSL_new (patch under Full configuration files).

  • Memory: wolfSSL reports ML-KEM-768 at about 32 KB stack and 12 KB heap with the default code. With --enable-smallstack it is about 2 KB stack and 27 KB heap. These were measured on a Raspberry Pi 5, not an MCU (Claimed, wolfSSL blog). Size TLS task stacks and receive buffers for a ClientHello of about 1.3 KB and a ServerHello of about 1.2 KB.

  • Test (Tested, wolfSSL 5.9.4, Alpine 3.24 package with WOLFSSL_HAVE_MLKEM): pqclient.c reached a PQ-only OpenSSL 3.5 server with group=X25519MLKEM768, and a classical-only server with group=X25519. The classical-only variant was refused by the PQ-only server, as expected (3/3).

Microcontrollers: Mbed TLS, ESP-IDF, Zephyr

Mbed TLS and TF-PSA-Crypto have no ML-KEM as of Mbed TLS 4.2.0 (July 2026). Trusted Firmware's minutes put ML-DSA first and "then look into ML-KEM" (Claimed). ESP-IDF esp_tls_cfg_t.groups_list takes only Mbed TLS groups. For PQ on ESP32, switch to wolfSSL with CONFIG_ESP_TLS_CUSTOM_STACK / esp_tls_register_stack(), or use wolfSSL's ESP-IDF examples. Devices that talk only to AWS IoT Core gain nothing from PQ until IoT Core supports it.

Linux-class devices and gateways: OpenSSL 3.5 and Mosquitto clients

On Debian 13 or Alpine 3.24, mosquitto_pub and mosquitto_sub offer X25519MLKEM768 first with no options. Mosquitto has no groups option. To restrict or enforce the groups, set OPENSSL_CONF for the process. Tested: mosquitto_pub reached a PQ-only broker with defaults. With OPENSSL_CONF limited to X25519/P-256 it failed with Error: Protocol error. For AL2023, Yocto and Buildroot images, see Hosts and OS.

AWS IoT Device SDK v2 (Python, JavaScript, Java, C++) via the AWS CRT

On Linux the CRT uses aws-c-io → s2n-tls + AWS-LC, bundled in the wheel, npm package or jar. Current aws-c-io maps the default to a PQ s2n policy (AWS-CRT-SDK-TLSv1.0-2025-PQ) and PQ_DEFAULT to AWS-CRT-SDK-TLSv1.2-2025-PQ (Documented, aws-c-io source).

Test (python:3.13-slim-trixie, awsiotsdk 1.31.0, awscrt 0.36.1)Result
cipher_pref = PQ_DEFAULT → PQ-only Mosquitto (mTLS)connected, published
cipher_pref = DEFAULT → PQ-only Mosquittoconnected (the default is already PQ on Linux)
cipher_pref = TLSv1_2_2025_07 (non-PQ) → PQ-only MosquittoAWS_IO_TLS_ERROR_NEGOTIATION_FAILURE, as expected
PQ_DEFAULT → normal Mosquitto (classical-capable)connected

To make PQ explicit in Python, set opts.cipher_pref = awscrt.io.TlsCipherPref.PQ_DEFAULT before ClientTlsContext(opts). In C++ the same enum value is AWS_IO_TLS_CIPHER_PREF_PQ_DEFAULT on Aws::Crt::Io::TlsContextOptions (setter name not verified). JS, Java and C++ weren't tested, but they use the same aws-c-io. Older awscrt versions have only PQ_TLSv1_0_2021_05, which is Kyber round 3 and deprecated: upgrade instead of selecting it. PKCS#11/TPM keys: aws-c-io uses legacy TLS 1.2 ELB policies for custom key operations and refuses TLS 1.3, so those devices get no PQ. Against IoT Core, the hybrid offer simply falls back to classical.

Greengrass v2, Android, OPC UA, LoRaWAN, cellular

  • Greengrass nucleus (Java): MQTT goes through aws-crt-java (0.45.0 in the current pom), so PQ is likely offered on Linux. This is inferred, not confirmed, and IoT Core is classical anyway. Component HTTPS calls follow the JDK (Java). Nucleus lite links the system OpenSSL, so use an OpenSSL 3.5 OS image (Debian 13, Alpine 3.24, or Yocto with OpenSSL 3.5).

  • Android gateways: whether Conscrypt has X25519MLKEM768 on by default per Android version is not confirmed; see Mobile, desktop and CLI clients.

  • OPC UA: no PQ SecurityPolicy exists (OPC 10000-2, 1.05.06). Over untrusted links, carry OPC UA in a PQ tunnel: strongSwan 6.0.2+ IPsec or a PQ TLS proxy (Network devices and egress).

  • LoRaWAN: AES-128 session keys and no public-key handshake, so ML-KEM doesn't apply on the radio link. The network server's cloud backhaul is ordinary TLS; treat it like a Linux gateway. No LoRa Alliance PQ statement found.

  • Cellular: 3GPP's PQ transition study is TR 33.703 (Release 20). There is no ML-KEM in 5G NAS/AS yet, so protect the IP payload with TLS or IPsec on top.

Verify

  1. Inventory: for each device model, record the TLS library and version and whether OTA is possible. Store them as thing attributes (for example tlsLib=wolfssl-5.9.4), then query fleet indexing for anything below wolfSSL 5.9.1, OpenSSL 3.5 or a current awscrt.

  2. Broker, PQ-only client must succeed: openssl s_client -connect broker:8883 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 -cert dev.pem -key dev.key -CAfile ca.pem -brief </dev/null prints Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768.

  3. Broker fallback: the same command with -groups X25519 must still connect, unless you enforce PQ.

  4. Device as client: point a test device at openssl s_server -accept 8883 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3 -cert srv.pem -key srv.key -CAfile ca.pem -Verify 1. It must complete the handshake. Against -groups X25519 it must fall back.

  5. Observed signal: the broker log (no suitable key share means a classical client was refused in PQ-only mode), a Zeek ssl.log curve on a mirrored gateway uplink (Network devices and egress), or wolfSSL_get_curve_name() / s2n_connection_get_kem_group_name() logged on the device.

Pitfalls and rollback

  • IoT Core is classical: don't hold device rollout back waiting for PQ on IoT Core. Ship PQ-capable stacks now, and enforce PQ on your own brokers and gateways first. Watch the IoT Core security policies page for a PQ policy. Device lifetimes of 10 years or more make procurement the cheapest point to fix this.

  • Buffers and stacks: a hybrid ClientHello is about 1.3 KB and the ServerHello about 1.2 KB. MCU TLS receive buffers of 1–2 KB, MQTT_NETWORK_BUFFER_SIZE and task stacks need headroom. Test on real hardware for heap fragmentation, handshake time and battery cost.

  • HelloRetryRequest: if the device lists the hybrid group but sends only an X25519 share, a PQ-only server forces an extra round trip. Send the hybrid key share first (wolfSSL_UseKeyShare).

  • PKCS#11 and secure-element keys: the CRT path gives no TLS 1.3 and so no PQ there. The alternative is wolfSSL with a crypto callback for the secure element.

  • Stale names: PQ_TLSv1_0_2021_05 (awscrt) and the Kyber IDs such as WOLFSSL_P521_KYBER_LEVEL5 are pre-standard, and servers no longer accept them. Replace them.

  • ESP-IDF registry lag: the managed wolfSSL component is 5.8.2, older than default-on ML-KEM. Pin a newer wolfSSL, or enable ML-KEM in user_settings.h, and test.

  • Rollback: brokers: remove the OPENSSL_CONF drop-in to return to hybrid-preferred with classical fallback. Devices: keep X25519/P-256 after the hybrid group so that fallback needs no change, and ship an OTA config flag that skips wolfSSL_UseKeyShare if a model misbehaves.

Full configuration files

Each file is complete. The label says whether it was Tested here, comes from vendor docs, or is an untested starting point.

user_settings.h (wolfSSL on an MCU. The PQ defines are from wolfSSL's examples/configs/user_settings_pq.h; the platform lines are a typical FreeRTOS/lwIP client profile. Not built on an MCU here: run wolfcrypt_test() on your port)

/* user_settings.h - wolfSSL for an MCU TLS 1.3 client with hybrid ML-KEM (X25519MLKEM768).
 * Compile with -DWOLFSSL_USER_SETTINGS. */
#ifndef WOLFSSL_USER_SETTINGS_H
#define WOLFSSL_USER_SETTINGS_H

/* Platform (adjust to your port) */
#define FREERTOS
#define WOLFSSL_LWIP
#define NO_FILESYSTEM
#define NO_WRITEV
#define SINGLE_THREADED            /* remove if several tasks use TLS */
#define WOLFSSL_SMALL_STACK        /* move big buffers to heap; ML-KEM needs it on MCUs */

/* TLS 1.3 client */
#define WOLFSSL_TLS13
#define NO_OLD_TLS
#define HAVE_TLS_EXTENSIONS
#define HAVE_SUPPORTED_CURVES
#define HAVE_SNI
#define HAVE_HKDF
#define HAVE_AESGCM
#define WOLFSSL_SHA384
#define WC_RSA_PSS
#define NO_WOLFSSL_SERVER          /* device is a client only */

/* Classical key exchange kept for fallback (IoT Core is classical) */
#define HAVE_ECC
#define ECC_TIMING_RESISTANT
#define HAVE_CURVE25519
#define TFM_TIMING_RESISTANT
#define WC_RSA_BLINDING

/* Post-quantum: ML-KEM (FIPS 203) and the hybrid groups */
#define WOLFSSL_HAVE_MLKEM
#define WOLFSSL_WC_MLKEM           /* native implementation */
#define WOLFSSL_SHA3
#define WOLFSSL_SHAKE128
#define WOLFSSL_SHAKE256
#define WOLFSSL_NO_ML_KEM_512      /* keep only ML-KEM-768 (X25519MLKEM768) */
#define WOLFSSL_NO_ML_KEM_1024
/* Lower RAM at some speed cost (wolfSSL memory blog): */
#define WOLFSSL_MLKEM_ENCAPSULATE_SMALL_MEM
#define WOLFSSL_MLKEM_MAKEKEY_SMALL_MEM

/* RNG: replace with your hardware TRNG hook */
/* #define CUSTOM_RAND_GENERATE_BLOCK my_trng_block */

#endif /* WOLFSSL_USER_SETTINGS_H */

pqclient.c (Tested, wolfSSL 5.9.4 on Alpine 3.24 against OpenSSL 3.5 servers. Build: cc pqclient.c -lwolfssl -o pqclient)

/* pqclient.c - wolfSSL TLS 1.3 client offering X25519MLKEM768 (hybrid) first.
 * Run: ./pqclient HOST PORT CAFILE [classic] */
#include <wolfssl/options.h>
#include <wolfssl/ssl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <netdb.h>
#include <sys/socket.h>
#include <unistd.h>

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    if (argc < 4) { fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s host port ca [classic]\n", argv[0]); return 2; }
    int classic = argc > 4 && strcmp(argv[4], "classic") == 0;
    struct addrinfo hints = {0}, *ai; hints.ai_socktype = SOCK_STREAM;
    if (getaddrinfo(argv[1], argv[2], &hints, &ai) != 0) return 2;
    int fd = socket(ai->ai_family, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (connect(fd, ai->ai_addr, ai->ai_addrlen) != 0) { perror("connect"); return 2; }

    wolfSSL_Init();
    WOLFSSL_CTX *ctx = wolfSSL_CTX_new(wolfTLSv1_3_client_method());
    wolfSSL_CTX_load_verify_locations(ctx, argv[3], NULL);
    /* Supported groups, in preference order. */
    int pq[] = { WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768, WOLFSSL_ECC_X25519, WOLFSSL_ECC_SECP256R1 };
    int cl[] = { WOLFSSL_ECC_X25519, WOLFSSL_ECC_SECP256R1 };
    if (wolfSSL_CTX_set_groups(ctx, classic ? cl : pq, classic ? 2 : 3) != WOLFSSL_SUCCESS)
        fprintf(stderr, "set_groups failed\n");
    WOLFSSL *ssl = wolfSSL_new(ctx);
    /* Key share sent in the first ClientHello (avoids a HelloRetryRequest round trip). */
    wolfSSL_UseKeyShare(ssl, classic ? WOLFSSL_ECC_X25519 : WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768);
    wolfSSL_UseSNI(ssl, WOLFSSL_SNI_HOST_NAME, argv[1], strlen(argv[1]));
    wolfSSL_set_fd(ssl, fd);
    if (wolfSSL_connect(ssl) != WOLFSSL_SUCCESS) {
        char e[80]; printf("HANDSHAKE_FAIL %s\n", wolfSSL_ERR_error_string(wolfSSL_get_error(ssl, 0), e));
        return 1;
    }
    printf("HANDSHAKE_OK version=%s group=%s\n", wolfSSL_get_version(ssl), wolfSSL_get_curve_name(ssl));
    wolfSSL_shutdown(ssl); wolfSSL_free(ssl); wolfSSL_CTX_free(ctx); close(fd);
    return 0;
}

Output: HANDSHAKE_OK version=TLSv1.3 group=X25519MLKEM768 (PQ-only server), HANDSHAKE_OK version=TLSv1.3 group=X25519 (classical-only server), and HANDSHAKE_FAIL received alert fatal error for the classic variant against the PQ-only server.

transport_wolfSSL.c addition (FreeRTOS coreMQTT, in TLS_FreeRTOS_Connect() after wolfSSL_new. Uses the same API calls as pqclient.c, but wasn't built in FreeRTOS here)

static int pqGroups[] = { WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768, WOLFSSL_ECC_X25519, WOLFSSL_ECC_SECP256R1 };

if( wolfSSL_set_groups( pxNetworkContext->ssl, pqGroups,
                        ( int ) ( sizeof( pqGroups ) / sizeof( pqGroups[ 0 ] ) ) ) != WOLFSSL_SUCCESS )
{
    LogWarn( ( "wolfSSL_set_groups failed; using library defaults." ) );
}
/* Send the hybrid share in ClientHello 1 (avoids a HelloRetryRequest with PQ-only brokers). */
if( wolfSSL_UseKeyShare( pxNetworkContext->ssl, WOLFSSL_X25519MLKEM768 ) != WOLFSSL_SUCCESS )
{
    LogWarn( ( "ML-KEM key share unavailable; is WOLFSSL_HAVE_MLKEM defined?" ) );
}
/* After wolfSSL_connect() succeeds, log what was negotiated: */
/* LogInfo( ( "TLS group: %s", wolfSSL_get_curve_name( pxNetworkContext->ssl ) ) ); */

/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf (Tested, Mosquitto 2.0.21 / OpenSSL 3.5.7; complete broker config)

# Mosquitto has no "groups" option: key exchange follows OpenSSL. On OpenSSL 3.5 the default
# list is X25519MLKEM768 first with classical fallback. To restrict groups, set OPENSSL_CONF
# for the mosquitto process (see openssl-pq-only.cnf / systemd drop-in).
per_listener_settings true

listener 8883
protocol mqtt
cafile   /etc/mosquitto/certs/ca.pem
certfile /etc/mosquitto/certs/server.pem
keyfile  /etc/mosquitto/certs/server.key
require_certificate true
use_identity_as_username true
# Allow TLS 1.2 for old devices; PQ needs TLS 1.3. Set tlsv1.3 to force 1.3 only.
tls_version tlsv1.2
allow_anonymous false

/etc/mosquitto/openssl-pq-only.cnf (Tested; enforces PQ for the broker, or for a client process)

# Use: OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/mosquitto/openssl-pq-only.cnf  (systemd: Environment=OPENSSL_CONF=...)
# For "prefer PQ, allow classical" use: Groups = X25519MLKEM768:X25519:secp256r1:secp384r1
openssl_conf = openssl_init

[openssl_init]
ssl_conf = ssl_module

[ssl_module]
system_default = tls_defaults

[tls_defaults]
MinProtocol = TLSv1.3
Groups = X25519MLKEM768

/etc/systemd/system/mosquitto.service.d/pq.conf (EC2 broker; enforces PQ. The OPENSSL_CONF mechanism was Tested; the systemd unit wasn't)

# Remove this file (systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart mosquitto) to roll back
# to OpenSSL 3.5 defaults: hybrid preferred, classical accepted.
[Service]
Environment=OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/mosquitto/openssl-pq-only.cnf

Dockerfile.mosquitto (ECS/EKS broker; not deployed)

FROM debian:trixie-slim@sha256:a72b4433de1cf7d6bae0c4cee74d0547f58601a643b3375f070c51600d63b6b2
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends mosquitto openssl ca-certificates \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY mosquitto.conf /etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf
COPY openssl-pq-only.cnf /etc/mosquitto/openssl-pq-only.cnf
# Certificates are mounted at /etc/mosquitto/certs (ECS secrets / EKS Secret volume).
# Set OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/mosquitto/openssl-pq-only.cnf in the task/pod env to enforce PQ.
USER mosquitto
EXPOSE 8883
ENTRYPOINT ["mosquitto", "-c", "/etc/mosquitto/mosquitto.conf"]

crt_mqtt_pq.py (Tested, awscrt 0.36.1 / awsiotsdk 1.31.0. Usage: python crt_mqtt_pq.py HOST PORT CA CERT KEY [PQ_DEFAULT|DEFAULT|TLSv1_2_2025_07])

"""MQTT over mutual TLS with the AWS CRT (aws-iot-device-sdk-python-v2 / awscrt).
On Linux, awscrt uses s2n-tls + AWS-LC; cipher_pref selects the s2n security policy."""
import sys
from awscrt import io, mqtt

host, port, ca, cert, key = sys.argv[1:6]
pref_name = sys.argv[6] if len(sys.argv) > 6 else "PQ_DEFAULT"

opts = io.TlsContextOptions.create_client_with_mtls_from_path(cert, key)
opts.override_default_trust_store_from_path(None, ca)
opts.cipher_pref = getattr(io.TlsCipherPref, pref_name)   # PQ_DEFAULT = hybrid ML-KEM offered
tls_ctx = io.ClientTlsContext(opts)

elg = io.EventLoopGroup(1)
resolver = io.DefaultHostResolver(elg)
bootstrap = io.ClientBootstrap(elg, resolver)
client = mqtt.Client(bootstrap, tls_ctx)
conn = mqtt.Connection(client=client, host_name=host, port=int(port),
                       client_id=f"crt-{pref_name}", clean_session=True, keep_alive_secs=30)
try:
    conn.connect().result(timeout=15)
    pub, _ = conn.publish(topic="pq/test", payload=b"hello", qos=mqtt.QoS.AT_LEAST_ONCE)
    pub.result(timeout=10)
    conn.disconnect().result(timeout=10)
    print(f"CONNECT_OK pref={pref_name}")
except Exception as e:  # noqa: BLE001
    print(f"CONNECT_FAIL pref={pref_name}: {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    sys.exit(1)

Dockerfile.gateway (Linux gateway with Device SDK v2 and Mosquitto clients on OpenSSL 3.5; the image and package versions are the tested ones, but the Dockerfile wasn't built)

FROM python:3.13-slim-trixie@sha256:e48f59cdba69a3cbd9ed2cf0f348d90d45a8d350d98134cf1070bc106ee9ed90
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends mosquitto-clients openssl ca-certificates \

RUN pip install --no-cache-dir "awsiotsdk==1.31.0" "awscrt==0.36.1"

Service mesh and east-west traffic

Linkerd 2.19+ is PQ for meshed traffic by default. Istio 1.27+ and Consul 2.1+ need one setting, and Istio's setting enforces PQ-only. Cilium's node encryption, ECS Service Connect and Kuma have no PQ key-exchange setting that we could find. App Mesh was shut down on 2026-09-30. Envoy configs and Kyverno guardrails were tested locally on 2026-11-14; no cluster was stood up.

What decides PQ here

The mesh proxy's TLS library and the group list the control plane pushes to it. The app talks plaintext to its local proxy, and proxy-to-proxy mTLS carries the hop: Envoy (BoringSSL) in Istio sidecars, Istio gateways, Consul and ECS Service Connect; the Rust proxies (Linkerd proxy, Istio ztunnel) use aws-lc. If the app does its own TLS, the mesh only forwards the encrypted bytes and the app's runtime decides (language tabs). Gateways and TLS origination to external hosts are "non-mesh TLS" and often have a separate setting. Certificate signatures stay classical in every mesh listed (Certificates (ML-DSA) tab).

Kuma / Kong MeshEnvoy mTLSNo PQ setting foundnone foundEKS, EC2Unverified

Lambda functions are not meshed; their outbound TLS is the language tabs.

Client side (app level)

Inside a mesh, the best client setting is none: send plaintext HTTP to the local proxy and let the mesh do mTLS. Then PQ follows the mesh row above, whatever language the app uses.

  • Calls to services inside the mesh: use http://svc.ns.svc.cluster.local. If the app uses https:// itself, the mesh only passes the bytes through, and the app's runtime picks the groups (Go, Python, Node.js, Java, .NET tabs).

  • Calls to external hosts (egress): either the app does TLS (language tab), or the app sends plain HTTP and Istio originates TLS with a ServiceEntry plus a DestinationRule in tls.mode: SIMPLE. Origination is non-mesh TLS, so it follows meshConfig.tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves or COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc.

    trafficPolicy:
  portLevelSettings:
  - port: { number: 443 }
    tls: { mode: SIMPLE, sni: api.partner.example, credentialName: partner-ca }

  • Linkerd: traffic to unmeshed or external destinations is not mesh mTLS; PQ there is the app's own TLS.

  • ECS without a PQ mesh: run a self-managed Envoy sidecar; the app calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/<service>/ and Envoy originates TLS with ecdh_curves (task definition and Dockerfile in Full configuration files; Envoy config in the Web servers tab).

Server side (mesh control plane and proxies)

  • Istio (enforcing, all proxy TLS): istiod Helm values pilot.env.COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc; ambient adds the ztunnel chart value env.COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc. Restart workloads so proxies reconnect.

    pilot:
  env:
    COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc

  • Istio (gateways only, with fallback): meshConfig.tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves: [X25519MLKEM768, X25519]. Use this for internet-facing gateways, because COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc also covers gateway downstream TLS and would refuse classical clients.

  • Linkerd 2.19+: nothing to set. helm upgrade linkerd-crds then linkerd-control-plane, then kubectl rollout restart each meshed workload.

  • Consul 2.1+: mesh config entry and agent TLS:

    Kind = "mesh"
TLS {
  Outgoing {
    TLSMinVersion = "TLSv1_3"
    TLSMaxVersion = "TLSv1_3"
    ECDHCurves    = ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"]
  }
}

    Incoming takes the same three keys. Agent tls.defaults: tls_min_version = "TLSv1_3" and tls_ecdh_curves = "X25519MLKEM768,X25519" (a comma-separated string, not a list). Allowed names: X25519MLKEM768, X25519, P-256, P-384, P-521.

  • Envoy self-managed: ecdh_curves: ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"] in both DownstreamTlsContext and UpstreamTlsContext (Tested; full file in the Web servers tab).

  • Cilium: keep IPsec per-tunnel keys (3+ prefix; global keys deprecated in 1.16) or WireGuard; neither gives PQ key exchange, so put PQ in a mesh layer above it when the threat model needs it.

Guardrails (Kyverno). The earlier ClusterPolicy version had three checks, run in Audit first: istiod and ztunnel must carry COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc; Envoy Gateway ClientTrafficPolicy.spec.tls.ecdhCurves must start with X25519MLKEM768; the ingress-nginx ConfigMap ssl-ecdh-curve must start with X25519MLKEM768. It passed on Kyverno CLI v1.16.0 (3 compliant resources passed, 3 non-compliant failed), but Kyverno 1.20 no longer runs kyverno.io/v1 ClusterPolicy (Tested: the 1.20 CLI rejects the file). Only the istiod check has been ported to the CEL ValidatingPolicy shown here (Tested, CLI 1.20.0); the ztunnel and Envoy Gateway checks are not ported yet, so on 1.20+ write them as ValidatingPolicy before relying on them. Gatekeeper equivalents were not written. Org-wide controls are in the Enforcement and guardrails tab.

Packaging per compute type

  • EKS (Istio): helm upgrade istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system -f values-istiod-pqc.yaml; ambient also helm upgrade ztunnel istio/ztunnel -n istio-system -f values-ztunnel-pqc.yaml. Rendering the 1.28.0 charts put COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc on the istiod container and tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves in the istio ConfigMap (Tested, helm template only). IstioOperator form is in Full configuration files.

  • EKS (Linkerd): chart version 2.19+ (or Buoyant Enterprise 2.19+); no values.

  • ECS / Fargate: Service Connect has no group setting, so for PQ between ECS services today use either app-level TLS (language tabs) or a self-managed Envoy sidecar: Dockerfile plus task definition in Terraform and CloudFormation below (CloudFormation passed cfn-lint; not deployed).

  • EC2 (Consul): agent tls.hcl in /etc/consul.d/, mesh entry with consul config write mesh.hcl, then restart the agent and Envoy sidecars.

Verify

  1. Posture. Istio: istioctl version 1.27+; kubectl -n istio-system get deploy istiod -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].env}' | grep COMPLIANCE_POLICY. Linkerd: linkerd version 2.19+ and linkerd check --proxy (all proxies on the new version). Consul: consul version 2.1+ and consul config read -kind mesh -name mesh.

  2. Envoy counters (Istio, Consul, self-managed). On fresh connections, ssl.curves.X25519MLKEM768 must rise and ssl.curves.X25519 must not. Tested on standalone Envoy 1.36: listener.0.0.0.0_8443.ssl.curves.X25519MLKEM768: 5 and cluster.be_pq.ssl.curves.X25519MLKEM768: 1.

    kubectl exec deploy/orders -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET 'stats?filter=ssl.curves'
kubectl exec deploy/orders -c istio-proxy -- pilot-agent request GET config_dump | grep -A3 ecdh_curves

  3. Linkerd. 2.19 exports the negotiated TLS key exchange as proxy metrics (announcement); check linkerd diagnostics proxy-metrics -n <ns> deploy/<name> for the key-exchange label. The exact metric name was not confirmed here.

  4. Gateways, live. From outside: openssl s_client -connect gw:443 -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 must show Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768; -groups X25519 must still connect unless you chose COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc, which refuses it.

  5. Envoy test results (2026-11-14). Envoy 1.36.13 and Istio's Envoy 1.36.3 with the Web servers tab config: 12 of 12 checks passed (PQ client, classical fallback, TLS 1.2 refused, PQ-only and classical backends reached). With ecdh_curves removed, the PQ-only client was refused and the PQ-only backend gave 503 (expected).

Pitfalls and rollback

  • COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc is PQ-only. It refuses peers without X25519MLKEM768: older Istio in multicluster, classical clients on ingress gateways, and external hosts reached by TLS origination. Turn it on per cluster after every peer is 1.27+; use tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves with fallback for internet-facing gateways.

  • tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves does not touch mesh mTLS and applies mesh-wide; there is no per-workload setting (Red Hat OSSM docs).

  • FIPS builds. Red Hat says PQC is unavailable on OpenShift clusters in FIPS mode. Envoy BoringSSL-FIPS before 1.40 defaults to P-256 only (Envoy's 1.40.0 changelog adds the hybrid to FIPS builds' defaults too, not tested here); Consul lists FIPS Envoy builds 1.38.4 and 1.39.1 that accept the hybrid group. Check your FIPS image before turning it on.

  • Envoy upstream maximum TLS defaults to 1.2: a TLS 1.3 minimum without a maximum fails with NO_SUPPORTED_VERSIONS_ENABLED (Tested). Consul notes the same.

  • Existing connections keep their groups until they close. Restart workloads or wait for connection churn before measuring.

  • Mixed versions (Linkerd proxies older than 2.19, Envoys without ML-KEM) negotiate classical silently with Linkerd and Consul fallback lists.

  • Apps doing their own TLS bypass all of this.

  • Rollback. Istio: remove COMPLIANCE_POLICY (and tlsDefaults.ecdhCurves), helm upgrade, restart istiod, ztunnel and workloads. Consul: set ECDHCurves = ["X25519"] and write the mesh entry. Linkerd: no switch to turn PQ off was found; downgrading below 2.19 is the only route (not recommended).

Full configuration files

values-istiod-pqc.yaml, values-ztunnel-pqc.yaml, istio-operator-pqc.yaml, egress-tls-origination.yaml (Istio)

# ---- values-istiod-pqc.yaml (helm upgrade istiod istio/istiod -n istio-system -f values-istiod-pqc.yaml) ----
# Rendered with helm template oci://gcr.io/istio-release/charts/istiod --version 1.28.0: env lands on the
# discovery container, tlsDefaults lands in the istio ConfigMap (checked 2026-11-14).
pilot:
  env:
    COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc          # Istio 1.27+: TLS 1.3 + X25519MLKEM768 only, for mesh mTLS, gateways and xDS
meshConfig:
  tlsDefaults:
    # Non-mesh TLS (gateway listeners, TLS origination). Used on its own when you want PQ-preferred
    # with classical fallback on gateways instead of the enforcing COMPLIANCE_POLICY.
    ecdhCurves: [X25519MLKEM768, X25519]
---
# ---- values-ztunnel-pqc.yaml (ambient only; helm upgrade ztunnel istio/ztunnel -n istio-system -f ...) ----
env:
  COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc
---
# ---- istio-operator-pqc.yaml (istioctl install -f istio-operator-pqc.yaml) ----
apiVersion: install.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: IstioOperator
metadata:
  name: pqc
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  profile: default                  # "ambient" for ambient mode
  meshConfig:
    tlsDefaults:
      ecdhCurves: [X25519MLKEM768, X25519]
  values:
    pilot:
      env:
        COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc
    ztunnel:                        # ambient profile only
      env:
        COMPLIANCE_POLICY: pqc
---
# ---- egress-tls-origination.yaml: app sends plain HTTP, the egress gateway / sidecar does PQ TLS to the external host ----
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata:
  name: partner-api
  namespace: payments
spec:
  hosts: [api.partner.example]
  ports:
  - number: 443
    name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
  resolution: DNS
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
---
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: partner-api-tls
  namespace: payments
spec:
  host: api.partner.example
  trafficPolicy:
    portLevelSettings:
    - port: { number: 443 }
      tls:
        mode: SIMPLE                # TLS origination; key-exchange groups from tlsDefaults / COMPLIANCE_POLICY
        sni: api.partner.example
        credentialName: partner-ca  # Secret with ca.crt; or caCertificates: /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt

mesh.hcl, mesh.yaml, /etc/consul.d/tls.hcl, systemd drop-in (Consul)

### mesh.hcl  (consul config write mesh.hcl) - Consul 2.1+
Kind = "mesh"
TLS {
  Incoming {
    TLSMinVersion = "TLSv1_3"
    TLSMaxVersion = "TLSv1_3"
    ECDHCurves    = ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"]
  }
  Outgoing {
    TLSMinVersion = "TLSv1_3"
    TLSMaxVersion = "TLSv1_3"   # set it: Envoy's upstream maximum otherwise defaults to TLS 1.2
    ECDHCurves    = ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"]
  }
}

### mesh.yaml  (Kubernetes, consul-k8s CRD; confirm with: kubectl explain mesh.spec.tls.incoming)
apiVersion: consul.hashicorp.com/v1alpha1
kind: Mesh
metadata:
  name: mesh
spec:
  tls:
    incoming:
      tlsMinVersion: TLSv1_3
      tlsMaxVersion: TLSv1_3
      ecdhCurves: ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"]
    outgoing:
      tlsMinVersion: TLSv1_3
      tlsMaxVersion: TLSv1_3
      ecdhCurves: ["X25519MLKEM768", "X25519"]

### /etc/consul.d/tls.hcl  (agent TLS: internal RPC, HTTPS, gRPC; Helm: server.extraConfig)
tls {
  defaults {
    ca_file         = "/etc/consul.d/certs/consul-agent-ca.pem"
    cert_file       = "/etc/consul.d/certs/server.pem"
    key_file        = "/etc/consul.d/certs/server-key.pem"
    verify_incoming = true
    verify_outgoing = true
    tls_min_version = "TLSv1_3"
    tls_ecdh_curves = "X25519MLKEM768,X25519"
  }
  internal_rpc {
    verify_server_hostname = true
  }
}

### /etc/systemd/system/consul.service.d/override.conf  (EC2)
[Service]
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/consul validate /etc/consul.d/

Dockerfile (self-managed Envoy sidecar for ECS; envoy.yaml is in the Web servers tab)

# Dockerfile - pq-envoy sidecar. Envoy 1.36.13 (BoringSSL) accepts X25519MLKEM768 (Tested 2026-11-14).
# The base image (Ubuntu 22.04) has no curl, which the ECS health check needs.
FROM envoyproxy/envoy@sha256:93e25ef06d87a908a1114e8dff9a2b3a3046fbbfda7e644d448d752332633de6
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# envoy.yaml = the Web servers tab file: listener 8443 terminates PQ TLS from peers,
# listener 8080 takes the app's plain HTTP and originates PQ TLS (ecdh_curves + TLS 1.3 min AND max) to peers.
COPY envoy.yaml /etc/envoy/envoy.yaml
# Certificates: write them to /certs at task start (e.g. an init container reading Secrets Manager);
# never bake private keys into the image.

ecs-envoy-sidecar.tf (Terraform)

# ecs-envoy-sidecar.tf - ECS/Fargate: self-managed Envoy sidecar doing PQ TLS for east-west calls,
# for teams that need PQ between ECS services today (Service Connect has no key-exchange setting).
# The app calls http://127.0.0.1:8080/<svc>/...; Envoy originates TLS with ecdh_curves to the peer task,
# and the peer's Envoy terminates on 8443. Image = envoyproxy/envoy with envoy.yaml baked in (Web servers tab).
variable "app_image" { type = string }
variable "envoy_image" { type = string } # e.g. <acct>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/pq-envoy@sha256:...
variable "execution_role_arn" { type = string }

resource "aws_ecs_task_definition" "orders" {
  family                   = "orders"
  requires_compatibilities = ["FARGATE"]
  network_mode             = "awsvpc"
  cpu                      = "512"
  memory                   = "1024"
  execution_role_arn       = var.execution_role_arn
  container_definitions = jsonencode([
    {
      name         = "app"
      image        = var.app_image
      essential    = true
      environment  = [{ name = "PAYMENTS_URL", value = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/payments" }]
      dependsOn    = [{ containerName = "envoy", condition = "HEALTHY" }]
      portMappings = []
    },
    {
      name         = "envoy"
      image        = var.envoy_image
      essential    = true
      command      = ["envoy", "-c", "/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml"]
      portMappings = [{ containerPort = 8443, protocol = "tcp" }]
      healthCheck = {
        command  = ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:9901/ready || exit 1"]
        interval = 10
        retries  = 3
      }
    }
  ])
}

ecs-envoy-sidecar.yaml (CloudFormation)

# ecs-envoy-sidecar.yaml - CloudFormation equivalent of ecs-envoy-sidecar.tf
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Parameters:
  AppImage: { Type: String }
  EnvoyImage: { Type: String }
  ExecutionRoleArn: { Type: String }
Resources:
  OrdersTask:
    Type: AWS::ECS::TaskDefinition
    Properties:
      Family: orders
      RequiresCompatibilities: [FARGATE]
      NetworkMode: awsvpc
      Cpu: "512"
      Memory: "1024"
      ExecutionRoleArn: !Ref ExecutionRoleArn
      ContainerDefinitions:
        - Name: app
          Image: !Ref AppImage
          Essential: true
          Environment:
            - Name: PAYMENTS_URL
              Value: http://127.0.0.1:8080/payments
          DependsOn:
            - ContainerName: envoy
              Condition: HEALTHY
        - Name: envoy
          Image: !Ref EnvoyImage
          Essential: true
          Command: [envoy, -c, /etc/envoy/envoy.yaml]
          PortMappings:
            - ContainerPort: 8443
              Protocol: tcp
          HealthCheck:
            Command: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -sf http://127.0.0.1:9901/ready || exit 1"]
            Interval: 10
            Retries: 3

kyverno-pq-policies.yaml (and the test resources in kyverno-test-resources.yaml under the work dir)

Tested (kyverno CLI 1.20)

apiVersion: policies.kyverno.io/v1
kind: ValidatingPolicy
metadata:
  name: pq-tls-istiod
spec:
  validationActions: [ Audit ]
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: [ apps ]
        apiVersions: [ v1 ]
        operations: [ CREATE, UPDATE ]
        resources: [ deployments ]
  matchConditions:
    - name: istiod
      expression: "object.metadata.namespace == 'istio-system' && object.metadata.name.startsWith('istiod')"
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.exists(c, c.name == 'discovery' && has(c.env) &&
        c.env.exists(e, e.name == 'COMPLIANCE_POLICY' && has(e.value) && e.value == 'pqc'))
      message: "PQ-K4: istiod container needs env COMPLIANCE_POLICY=pqc"

Full policy set: see the Enforcement and guardrails tab.

Databases and data services

What decides PQ here

Two TLS stacks meet on every database connection. The server engine (its version, its group setting and the TLS library it links) decides which groups it accepts; the client driver's TLS stack decides which groups it offers. Hybrid X25519MLKEM768 needs both sides to support it, TLS 1.3, and no setting on either side that pins a classical list.

On managed services AWS owns the server stack, so you change a parameter group or the engine version. On self-managed engines you choose the image and set the engine's group option, or an OpenSSL config file where the engine has none. Tests in this tab ran on 2026-11-14 (arm64 Docker); scripts and output are kept in the data work directory.

Client side (app level)

The driver's TLS stack decides what the client offers. Runtime rules live in the language tabs: Go, Python, Node.js, Java, .NET. Database-specific points:

No libpq connection parameter for groups was found (not confirmed); use OPENSSL_CONF (see openssl-groups.cnf in Full configuration files) if you must change the client's list.

Clients linked to GnuTLS instead of OpenSSL get no ML-KEM, even on Debian 13 or Ubuntu 26.04: wget and libcurl-gnutls fail against a PQ-only server (Tested by another group for this document). Run ldd on any database client or tool before relying on the OS version.

Server side

RDS for PostgreSQL 18 and Aurora PostgreSQL 18

  • Parameter group family postgres18 (RDS instance) or aurora-postgresql18 (Aurora, cluster parameter group).

  • ssl_groups: hybrid first, classical after for fallback: X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768,X25519,prime256v1. Use commas in the API, Terraform and CloudFormation (Claimed: the RDS API rejects colon lists).

  • rds.force_ssl = 1 (default on 15+).

  • To enforce PQ: ssl_groups = X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768 and ssl_min_protocol_version = TLSv1.3, because ML-KEM needs TLS 1.3 (Documented).

aws rds modify-db-parameter-group --db-parameter-group-name pg18-pq \
  --parameters "ParameterName=ssl_groups,ParameterValue='X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768,X25519,prime256v1',ApplyMethod=immediate"

Full Terraform and CloudFormation are in Full configuration files.

RDS and Aurora MySQL, RDS for MariaDB

  • Aurora MySQL: upgrade to 8.4.8+ (8.4-compatible line) or 3.14.0+ (8.0-compatible line); no parameter. Check SHOW STATUS LIKE 'Aurora_ssl_named_group'. Keep require_secure_transport = ON and tls_version = TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3; TLS 1.2 clients stay classical.

  • RDS for MySQL 8.4.11 and RDS for MariaDB (12.3.3, 11.4.13, 11.8.9): upgrade the minor version. The enabling parameter is not confirmed here. After the upgrade, list the parameter group for a groups or PQ parameter and probe with s_client (Verify).

Self-managed PostgreSQL 18 (Tested)

# postgresql.conf (excerpt)
ssl = on
ssl_groups = 'X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1'   # PG 18 name; ssl_ecdh_curve is an alias
ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2'               # 'TLSv1.3' to enforce PQ

hostssl lines in pg_hba.conf reject non-TLS clients. SELECT pg_reload_conf(); applies TLS settings to new connections.

Self-managed MySQL

  • 8.4 LTS and 9.x: no PQ on the server, even linked to OpenSSL 3.5.8 (Tested). Plan for MySQL 26.x.

  • 26.x: PQ on by default (Tested). Variables (Documented, MySQL 26.10 manual): tls_kex (colon list, case-sensitive names), force_pqc, use_pqc_sign, each with admin_, replication_, group_replication_ and mysqlx_ variants. Status: Tls_key_exchange_algorithm, Tls_sign_algorithm.

  • Version history: server-side PQC (PQ groups, force_pqc) was added in MySQL 26.7.0 (MySQL 26.7 manual, Documented); 26.10 adds the MySQL Shell and client options tls-kex and force-pqc. Any 26.7+ server qualifies; the tests here used 26.10.

# my.cnf (excerpt)
[mysqld]
require_secure_transport = ON
tls_version = TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3
tls_kex = X25519MLKEM768:secp256r1MLKEM768:X25519:secp256r1
# force_pqc = ON          # enforcement: classical clients fail (Tested)

Self-managed MariaDB, Valkey, Redis OSS

No group option of their own was found. They follow OpenSSL's defaults, which on OpenSSL 3.5 put X25519MLKEM768 first. To change the order or enforce PQ-only, point OPENSSL_CONF at a file with Groups = ... (Tested on Valkey 8.1.11: the PQ-only file rejected an X25519-only client).

# valkey.conf (excerpt)
port 0
tls-port 6379
tls-cert-file /etc/valkey/tls/server.crt
tls-key-file  /etc/valkey/tls/server.key
tls-ca-cert-file /etc/valkey/tls/ca.crt
tls-protocols "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"

Kafka and Cassandra (JVM)

The broker's JDK decides. Run JDK 25.0.5+ (PQ by default) or attach the Bouncy Castle JSSE agent from the Java tab. Kafka: ssl.enabled.protocols=TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2. To pin groups, set -Djdk.tls.namedGroups=X25519MLKEM768,x25519,secp256r1 in KAFKA_OPTS. Not tested on a broker (Unverified).

Packaging per compute type

Database servers do not run on Lambda; database clients do, so follow the language tab for each runtime. For engines you run yourself:

Where the engine runsWhat to shipEvidence
ECS/Fargate or EKSAn image with OpenSSL 3.5: postgres:18 (Debian 13), mysql:26, mariadb:13 (Ubuntu 26.04), valkey/valkey:8 or :8-alpine. Pin by digest. Config by container args, file mount or baked-in file.Tested (images)
EC2 on AL2023OpenSSL 3.5 is present but the crypto policy omits ML-KEM (see Hosts and OS). Set ssl_groups explicitly (PostgreSQL) or OPENSSL_CONF in the service's systemd drop-in.Unverified for database daemons on AL2023
Client containersDebian 13 or Alpine 3.24 bases; avoid -bookworm tags (OpenSSL 3.0)Tested

The EKS StatefulSet, ECS task definition and systemd drop-in are in Full configuration files.

Verify

  1. Posture: engine version and parameter values.

aws rds describe-db-parameters --db-parameter-group-name pg18-pq \
  --query "Parameters[?ParameterName=='ssl_groups'].[ParameterValue]" --output text
psql "host=$H sslmode=verify-full sslrootcert=global-bundle.pem" -c "SHOW ssl_groups"

  1. Live test from a host with OpenSSL 3.5, for example a debian:trixie-slim task in the same VPC. PQ must succeed; classical must still work (fallback).

# PostgreSQL
openssl s_client -connect $H:5432 -starttls postgres -tls1_3 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -brief </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect $H:5432 -starttls postgres -groups X25519 -brief </dev/null
# MySQL / MariaDB
openssl s_client -connect $H:3306 -starttls mysql -groups X25519MLKEM768 -brief </dev/null
# Valkey / Redis (direct TLS)
openssl s_client -connect $H:6379 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -brief </dev/null

Expect Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768 for the PQ run and Peer Temp Key: X25519 for the classical one (Tested on every self-managed engine above).

  1. Observed signal on the server:

  • PostgreSQL: log_connections prints protocol, cipher and bits, not the group (Tested); pg_stat_ssl has no group column. Use the probe.

  • MySQL 26: SHOW SESSION STATUS LIKE 'Tls_key_exchange_algorithm' (Tested). Aurora MySQL: Aurora_ssl_named_group (Documented in the 3.14.0 notes).

  • Valkey, MariaDB: no server-side field; use the probe.

Pitfalls and rollback

  • Fallback is silent. A Debian 12 libpq client still connects to a PQ-first server using X25519 (Tested). Only enforcement (PQ-only groups, force_pqc) exposes it, by breaking it.

  • Server order is not always obeyed. With OpenSSL 3.5, a client that sent only an X25519 key share got X25519 although the server listed ML-KEM first (Tested on Valkey); OpenSSL avoids a HelloRetryRequest. Fix the client, or enforce.

  • Self-managed MySQL 8.4 and 9.x cannot be fixed with OpenSSL 3.5 alone; the server sticks to P-256 (Tested).

  • Official MariaDB images before 13 run on Ubuntu 24.04 with OpenSSL 3.0: no PQ (Tested).

  • RDS Proxy terminates TLS; that leg stays classical. Bypass it for sensitive data or record an exception.

  • ML-KEM needs TLS 1.3. Clients or servers pinned to TLS 1.2 stay classical.

  • Rollback: set ssl_groups back to prime256v1:X25519 (dynamic, new connections only), set force_pqc=OFF, or remove OPENSSL_CONF and restart. Existing sessions are not dropped.

Full configuration files

postgresql.conf (TLS section)

# /var/lib/postgresql/data/postgresql.conf  (PostgreSQL 18, OpenSSL 3.5) - TLS section
listen_addresses = '*'
ssl = on
ssl_cert_file = '/etc/postgresql/tls/server.crt'
ssl_key_file  = '/etc/postgresql/tls/server.key'        # mode 0600, owner postgres
ssl_ca_file   = '/etc/postgresql/tls/ca.crt'            # only for client-certificate auth
ssl_min_protocol_version = 'TLSv1.2'                    # 'TLSv1.3' to enforce PQ
ssl_groups = 'X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1'         # PQ-only: 'X25519MLKEM768'
log_connections = on

pg_hba.conf

# /var/lib/postgresql/data/pg_hba.conf - TLS required for remote clients
# TYPE    DATABASE  USER  ADDRESS       METHOD
local     all       all                 peer
hostssl   all       all   10.0.0.0/8    scram-sha-256
hostnossl all       all   0.0.0.0/0     reject

rds-pg-pq.tf (Terraform: RDS instance and Aurora cluster parameter groups)

# rds-pg-pq.tf - hybrid PQ key exchange for RDS for PostgreSQL 18 and Aurora PostgreSQL 18
variable "enforce_pq" {
  type    = bool
  default = false
}

locals {
  ssl_groups = var.enforce_pq ? "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768" : "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768,X25519,prime256v1"
  min_tls    = var.enforce_pq ? "TLSv1.3" : "TLSv1.2"
}

resource "aws_db_parameter_group" "pg18_pq" {
  name   = "pg18-pq"
  family = "postgres18"

  parameter {
    name         = "ssl_groups"
    value        = local.ssl_groups
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "ssl_min_protocol_version"
    value        = local.min_tls
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "rds.force_ssl"
    value        = "1"
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group" "aurora_pg18_pq" {
  name   = "aurora-pg18-pq"
  family = "aurora-postgresql18"

  parameter {
    name         = "ssl_groups"
    value        = local.ssl_groups
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "ssl_min_protocol_version"
    value        = local.min_tls
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
  parameter {
    name         = "rds.force_ssl"
    value        = "1"
    apply_method = "immediate"
  }
}

# Attach: aws_db_instance.parameter_group_name = aws_db_parameter_group.pg18_pq.name
#         aws_rds_cluster.db_cluster_parameter_group_name = aws_rds_cluster_parameter_group.aurora_pg18_pq.name

rds-pg-pq.yaml (CloudFormation)

# rds-pg-pq.yaml - hybrid PQ key exchange parameter groups for PostgreSQL 18
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Parameters:
  EnforcePq:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: ["true", "false"]
    Default: "false"
Conditions:
  Enforce: !Equals [!Ref EnforcePq, "true"]
Resources:
  Pg18PqParams:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: postgres18
      Description: RDS PostgreSQL 18 hybrid ML-KEM key exchange
      Parameters:
        ssl_groups: !If [Enforce, "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768", "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768,X25519,prime256v1"]
        ssl_min_protocol_version: !If [Enforce, "TLSv1.3", "TLSv1.2"]
        rds.force_ssl: "1"
  AuroraPg18PqParams:
    Type: AWS::RDS::DBClusterParameterGroup
    Properties:
      Family: aurora-postgresql18
      Description: Aurora PostgreSQL 18 hybrid ML-KEM key exchange
      Parameters:
        ssl_groups: !If [Enforce, "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768", "X25519MLKEM768,SecP256r1MLKEM768,X25519,prime256v1"]
        ssl_min_protocol_version: !If [Enforce, "TLSv1.3", "TLSv1.2"]
        rds.force_ssl: "1"
Outputs:
  InstanceParameterGroup:
    Value: !Ref Pg18PqParams
  ClusterParameterGroup:
    Value: !Ref AuroraPg18PqParams

tls-pq.cnf (MySQL 26.x)

# /etc/my.cnf.d/tls-pq.cnf - MySQL 26.x built with OpenSSL 3.5
[mysqld]
ssl_ca   = /etc/mysql/tls/ca.crt
ssl_cert = /etc/mysql/tls/server.crt
ssl_key  = /etc/mysql/tls/server.key
require_secure_transport = ON
tls_version = TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3
tls_kex = X25519MLKEM768:secp256r1MLKEM768:X25519:secp256r1
replication_tls_kex = X25519MLKEM768:X25519
# Enforcement (classical clients fail; TLS 1.2-only configs are rejected):
# force_pqc = ON
# replication_force_pqc = ON

[client]
ssl-mode = VERIFY_IDENTITY
ssl-ca   = /etc/mysql/tls/ca.crt
tls-kex  = X25519MLKEM768:X25519

90-tls.cnf (MariaDB 13 on OpenSSL 3.5)

# /etc/mysql/mariadb.conf.d/90-tls.cnf
[mariadbd]
ssl_ca   = /etc/mysql/tls/ca.crt
ssl_cert = /etc/mysql/tls/server.crt
ssl_key  = /etc/mysql/tls/server.key
require_secure_transport = ON
tls_version = TLSv1.2,TLSv1.3
# Groups come from OpenSSL: X25519MLKEM768 first by default on OpenSSL 3.5.
# To change order or enforce PQ-only, set OPENSSL_CONF (see openssl-groups.cnf).

valkey.conf (TLS section)

# /etc/valkey/valkey.conf - TLS section (Valkey 8.x on OpenSSL 3.5)
port 0
tls-port 6379
tls-cert-file /etc/valkey/tls/server.crt
tls-key-file  /etc/valkey/tls/server.key
tls-ca-cert-file /etc/valkey/tls/ca.crt
tls-auth-clients optional
tls-protocols "TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3"
tls-replication yes
tls-cluster yes
# Group order: OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/ssl/openssl-groups.cnf in the service environment

openssl-groups.cnf (process-wide groups for daemons without a group option)

# /etc/ssl/openssl-groups.cnf - use with OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/ssl/openssl-groups.cnf
# OpenSSL 3.5+ (Debian 13, Alpine 3.22+, Ubuntu 26.04). Tested with Valkey 8.1.11.
openssl_conf = openssl_init

[openssl_init]
ssl_conf = ssl_module
providers = provider_sect

[provider_sect]
default = default_sect

[default_sect]
activate = 1

[ssl_module]
system_default = tls_defaults

[tls_defaults]
MinProtocol = TLSv1.2
Groups = X25519MLKEM768:X25519:secp256r1:secp384r1
# PQ-only enforcement variant (openssl-pq-only.cnf, Tested):
#   MinProtocol = TLSv1.3
#   Groups = X25519MLKEM768

server.properties (Kafka TLS listener; Unverified)

# /opt/kafka/config/server.properties - TLS listener (broker on JDK 25.0.5+)
listeners=SSL://:9093
security.inter.broker.protocol=SSL
ssl.enabled.protocols=TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2
ssl.protocol=TLSv1.3
ssl.keystore.type=PKCS12
ssl.keystore.location=/opt/kafka/tls/broker.p12
ssl.keystore.password=${file:/opt/kafka/tls/secrets.properties:keystore.password}
ssl.truststore.type=PKCS12
ssl.truststore.location=/opt/kafka/tls/truststore.p12

postgres-pq.yaml (EKS StatefulSet)

# postgres-pq.yaml - PostgreSQL 18 on EKS with hybrid PQ groups (same -c flags as the tests)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: postgres
spec:
  serviceName: postgres
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: postgres }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: postgres }
    spec:
      securityContext:
        fsGroup: 999
      containers:
        - name: postgres
          image: postgres:18   # Debian 13, OpenSSL 3.5.x; pin by digest for your architecture
          args:
            - "-c"
            - "ssl=on"
            - "-c"
            - "ssl_cert_file=/etc/postgresql/tls/tls.crt"
            - "-c"
            - "ssl_key_file=/etc/postgresql/tls/tls.key"
            - "-c"
            - "ssl_min_protocol_version=TLSv1.2"
            - "-c"
            - "ssl_groups=X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1"
          env:
            - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
              valueFrom: { secretKeyRef: { name: postgres-auth, key: password } }
            - name: PGDATA
              value: /var/lib/postgresql/data/pgdata
          ports: [{ containerPort: 5432 }]
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: tls, mountPath: /etc/postgresql/tls, readOnly: true }
            - { name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/postgresql/data }
      volumes:
        - name: tls
          secret: { secretName: postgres-tls-cert, defaultMode: 0640 }
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        resources: { requests: { storage: 20Gi } }

10-pq-groups.conf (systemd drop-in, EC2)

# /etc/systemd/system/valkey.service.d/10-pq-groups.conf

Then systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart valkey.

Hosts and operating systems

What decides PQ here

The host OS decides PQ only for programs that use the system TLS library: OpenSSL, GnuTLS or NSS on Linux, Schannel on Windows, Apple's stack on macOS. On Red Hat-family systems (AL2023, RHEL) the system-wide crypto policy writes the group list for all three Linux libraries and for OpenSSH. Programs that bring their own TLS (Go, Java, the official Node.js binaries, rustls, AWS CLI v2) follow the language tabs whatever the host is.

Status matrix

Tested = run here on 2026-11-14 in containers against a PQ-only openssl s_server (-groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3) and a classical-only one (-groups X25519), plus sshd restricted to one key exchange. Scripts and output: deep/hosts/run-hosts*.sh and run-hosts*.out in the work dir.

Bottlerocket

Bottlerocket has no package manager and no crypto-policies tool, and I couldn't confirm which OpenSSL version its core kit ships (searched release notes 2026-11-14). That matters little in practice:

  • Workload TLS comes from the container image, not the host.

  • Host agents (containerd, kubelet, ecs-agent, the SSM agent in the control container) are Go programs; current Go builds offer X25519MLKEM768 by default. Not confirmed per Bottlerocket version.

  • The admin and control containers can't be retuned in a supported way. Treat any TLS they make as unknown until Bottlerocket documents it.

Not testable here (needs a Bottlerocket VM).

Per-service override with systemd

On AL2023, to change one service and not the whole host, point that unit at the PQ config. Tested equivalent: with the policy at DEFAULT, curl run with OPENSSL_CONF=/tmp/openssl-pq.cnf negotiated X25519MLKEM768 and still reached the classical server.

# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service.d/pq-tls.conf (excerpt)
[Service]
Environment=OPENSSL_CONF=/etc/pki/tls/openssl-pq.cnf

Then systemctl daemon-reload && systemctl restart myapp. Only OpenSSL-linked programs read this variable.

OpenSSH client

OpenSSH ≥ 10.0 puts mlkem768x25519-sha256 first by default (OpenSSH PQ); nothing to set. For 9.9 hosts, or to pin the order:

# ~/.ssh/config or /etc/ssh/ssh_config.d/40-pq-kex.conf (excerpt)
Host *
    KexAlgorithms mlkem768x25519-sha256,sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com,curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org

OpenSSH before 9.9 rejects the unknown name and exits; on 9.0–9.8 (Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12) put sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com first instead. sntrup761 is not a NIST algorithm; use it only as an interim step.

Server side

Amazon Linux 2023: crypto policy

  1. Patch to AL2023.12 or later.

  2. dnf -y install crypto-policies-scripts && dnf -y update crypto-policies crypto-policies-scripts.

  3. update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:PQ (FIPS:PQ on FIPS hosts).

  4. Restart services, or reboot. Already-running processes keep the old list.

Tested on AL2023.12.20261102. At DEFAULT, OpenSSL's Groups line is *X25519:secp256r1:… and both curl and s_client fail on the PQ-only server. At DEFAULT:PQ it becomes *?X25519MLKEM768:?x25519_mlkem768:?SecP256r1MLKEM768:…/*X25519:…; curl reports X25519MLKEM768; the classical server still works; sshd -T and the ssh client list mlkem768x25519-sha256 first; GnuTLS lists GROUP-X25519-MLKEM768 first.

DEFAULT:PQ also enables ML-DSA signatures and the P-256/P-384 ML-KEM hybrids. For the smallest change, use a custom subpolicy that adds only the X25519 hybrid group:

# /etc/crypto-policies/policies/modules/PQ-HYBRID.pmod
group = +X25519-MLKEM768

Apply with update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:PQ-HYBRID. Tested: OpenSSL's Groups line became *?X25519MLKEM768:?x25519_mlkem768/*X25519:… and curl negotiated X25519MLKEM768. (AL2023's own PQ.pmod spells the group MLKEM768-X25519; the tested spelling above also works.)

OpenSSH server

HostWhat to doEvidence

Debian 13, Ubuntu 26.04, Alpine 3.24, RHEL 10.1Nothing: OpenSSH 10.x prefers ML-KEM by defaultDocumented; client side Tested
Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12Upgrade the OS; sntrup761 meanwhileTested

To restrict a server to PQ only (a bastion, or an SFTP host for PQ clients):

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/40-pq-kex.conf (excerpt; not on AL2023, where the policy owns this)
KexAlgorithms mlkem768x25519-sha256,sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com

Tested on Debian 13 sshd with -o KexAlgorithms=mlkem768x25519-sha256: OpenSSH 9.9+ clients connected with ML-KEM; Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 12 and AL2023-at-DEFAULT clients failed with no matching key exchange method found.

Session Manager and EC2 Instance Connect

  • Session Manager doesn't use sshd; the SSM agent opens a TLS WebSocket to ssmmessages. The agent is Go 1.26 (offers PQ) but that endpoint isn't on AWS's PQ list. Assume classical (AWS service endpoints).

  • EC2 Instance Connect pushes a key through a PQ-capable API, then you SSH to the instance's sshd: the sshd rules above apply.

Web servers and other daemons on the host

nginx, Apache httpd, HAProxy and Postfix linked to the system OpenSSL follow the crypto policy unless their config sets groups. Server config: Web servers and proxies.

Windows Server 2025 (Schannel)

  1. Install KB5099536 (2026-07-14) or later.

  2. Enable-TlsEccCurve -Name "X25519_MLKEM768" -Position 0 (elevated). Microsoft says position 0 is needed for it to be negotiated.

  3. TLS 1.3 must be on. Group Policy overrides the PowerShell setting, so pick one ("don't mix-n-match", Microsoft).

  4. Restart services that hold TLS contexts. Whether a reboot is needed isn't stated; not confirmed.

Windows Server 2022 and 2019 have no announced PQ Schannel. For PQ on those hosts, terminate TLS in front of them (Load balancers, Edge and API front doors) or move to 2025.

  1. Posture (SSM Run Command or Inventory): update-crypto-policies --show = DEFAULT:PQ; grep Groups /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensslcnf.config starts with *?X25519MLKEM768; sshd -T | grep ^kexalgorithms starts with mlkem768x25519-sha256; rpm -q openssl-libs openssh-server (≥ 3.5, ≥ 9.9). Windows: Get-TlsEccCurve lists X25519_MLKEM768 first.

  2. Live: from the host, openssl s_client -connect pq-test:443 -brief (no -groups, so the policy is what's tested) must print Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768; a classical server must still connect. ssh -v host true 2>&1 | grep 'kex: algorithm' must print mlkem768x25519-sha256.

  3. Observed: CloudTrail tlsDetails.keyExchange for the host's AWS calls made by a system-OpenSSL client; Zeek on VPC Traffic Mirroring for other host traffic; ALB connection logs for calls to your ALBs.

Pitfalls and rollback

  • DEFAULT:PQ changes every OpenSSL, GnuTLS, NSS and OpenSSH program at once, including dnf, agent helpers and monitoring agents. Roll out in waves by tag.

  • Rollback: update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT, then restart. Tested: the PQ-only server failed again right after rollback.

  • Debian/Ubuntu GnuTLS programs stay classical even on Debian 13 and Ubuntu 26.04 (Tested). Don't assume wget or git follow curl.

  • OpenSSH config: mlkem768x25519-sha256 in ssh_config on OpenSSH < 9.9 breaks every ssh call. Gate by version.

  • Middleboxes: the larger ClientHello can be dropped by old inspection devices. Test each fleet's egress path before its wave (Network devices and egress).

  • AL2 hosts can't be fixed. They're past end of support (2026-06-30); migrate to AL2023.

Full configuration files

The policy commands, subpolicy, OPENSSL_CONF file and sshd/ssh settings were Tested in containers. The SSM documents, Terraform and CloudFormation wrap those commands and were not applied to an AWS account.

ssm/PQ-SetCryptoPolicy.json (SSM Command document, AL2023 and RHEL 9.7+)

{
  "schemaVersion": "2.2",
  "description": "Set the system-wide crypto policy (PQ rollout or rollback) and report the result.",
  "parameters": {
    "Policy": {
      "type": "String",
      "default": "DEFAULT:PQ",
      "allowedValues": ["DEFAULT:PQ", "FIPS:PQ", "DEFAULT:PQ-HYBRID", "DEFAULT", "FIPS"]
    },
    "RestartUnits": {
      "type": "String",
      "default": "sshd",
      "description": "Space-separated systemd units to restart after the change"
    }
  },
  "mainSteps": [
    {
      "action": "aws:runShellScript",
      "name": "setCryptoPolicy",
      "precondition": { "StringEquals": ["platformType", "Linux"] },
      "inputs": {
        "timeoutSeconds": "600",
        "runCommand": [
          "set -eu",
          "command -v dnf >/dev/null || { echo 'not a dnf-based host'; exit 0; }",
          "dnf -y -q install crypto-policies-scripts",
          "dnf -y -q update crypto-policies crypto-policies-scripts",
          "if [ '{{ Policy }}' = 'DEFAULT:PQ-HYBRID' ]; then printf 'group = +X25519-MLKEM768\\n' > /etc/crypto-policies/policies/modules/PQ-HYBRID.pmod; fi",
          "current=$(update-crypto-policies --show)",
          "if [ \"$current\" != '{{ Policy }}' ]; then update-crypto-policies --set '{{ Policy }}'; for u in {{ RestartUnits }}; do systemctl try-restart \"$u\" || true; done; fi",
          "echo \"policy=$(update-crypto-policies --show)\"",
          "grep -m1 -i '^Groups' /etc/crypto-policies/back-ends/opensslcnf.config || true",
          "sshd -T 2>/dev/null | grep -i '^kexalgorithms' | cut -c1-120 || true",
          "rpm -q openssl-libs openssh-server || true"
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

ssm/pq-policy.tf (Terraform: document, a wave association and a rollback association)

resource "aws_ssm_document" "pq_policy" {
  name            = "PQ-SetCryptoPolicy"
  document_type   = "Command"
  document_format = "JSON"
  content         = file("${path.module}/PQ-SetCryptoPolicy.json")
}

resource "aws_ssm_association" "pq_wave" {
  name                = aws_ssm_document.pq_policy.name
  association_name    = "pq-crypto-policy-wave1"
  schedule_expression = "rate(1 day)"
  max_concurrency     = "10%"
  max_errors          = "5%"
  parameters = {
    Policy       = "DEFAULT:PQ"
    RestartUnits = "sshd"
  }
  targets {
    key    = "tag:PQRollout"
    values = ["wave1"]
  }
}

resource "aws_ssm_association" "pq_rollback" {
  name             = aws_ssm_document.pq_policy.name
  association_name = "pq-crypto-policy-rollback"
  max_concurrency  = "25%"
  max_errors       = "10%"
  parameters = {
    Policy       = "DEFAULT"
    RestartUnits = "sshd"
  }
  targets {
    key    = "tag:PQRollout"
    values = ["rollback"]
  }
}

Certificates and signatures (ML-DSA)

What decides PQ here

ML-DSA (FIPS 204) replaces the signatures in certificates; it is the second step after ML-KEM key exchange. It is less urgent: recorded traffic can be decrypted later, but a signature only has to hold at the moment of the handshake. Today ML-DSA works in private PKI only.

Three parties decide whether a handshake uses an ML-DSA certificate. The CA must sign with ML-DSA. The server must hold an ML-DSA certificate and a TLS library that can sign with it (OpenSSL 3.5+). The client must offer ML-DSA in its signature_algorithms extension and be able to verify the chain. A server that also holds an ECDSA certificate falls back to it for clients that don't offer ML-DSA; that dual-certificate setup is the safe way to start (Tested 2026-11-14).

ML-KEM (key exchange)ML-DSA (signatures, certificates)
ThreatTraffic recorded today, decrypted laterForged certificates once a quantum computer exists
UrgencyNowLater
What changesTLS libraries and config at both endsThe CA, every certificate, every verifier
Where it worksMost of this documentPrivate PKI only

Size cost (Tested, DER): ML-DSA-87 root 7,510 bytes, ML-DSA-65 intermediate 6,876, ML-DSA-44 leaf 4,953; ECDSA P-256 root 424 and leaf 464. Leaf plus intermediate grows from about 0.9 KB to 11.8 KB. An ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 bytes and its public key 1,312 bytes, against 64 bytes for an ECDSA P-256 signature.

Client side (app level)

A client needs the private root in its trust store and, to receive the ML-DSA certificate, a TLS stack that offers ML-DSA. Clients that have only the root still work against a dual-certificate server; they receive ECDSA.

RuntimeTrust the private rootNotes
OpenSSL tools, curl, libpq, Valkey--cacert / sslrootcert=; or the system store: Debian/Alpine /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/*.crt + update-ca-certificates; AL2023 /etc/pki/ca-trust/source/anchors/ + update-ca-trustOpenSSL 3.5 offers mldsa44/65/87 by default (seen in a ClientHello trace, Tested)
Pythonssl.create_default_context(cafile=...); SSL_CERT_FILE; requests: REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE (certifi has no private roots)Python must link OpenSSL 3.5 (Python tab)
Node.jstls.connect({ ca }); NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/root.pemNode 24 bundles OpenSSL 3.5 (Tested)
Gox509.NewCertPool() + AppendCertsFromPEM; SSL_CERT_FILEGo 1.27 verifies ML-DSA chains; crypto/tls never selects ML-DSA, so the server must also hold ECDSA
JavaPKCS12 truststore (javax.net.ssl.trustStore)Stock JDK 25 validates ML-DSA chains, but JSSE negotiates ECDSA
.NETX509ChainPolicy.CustomTrustStore with TrustMode = CustomRootTrust, or the OS storeLinux needs OpenSSL 3.5; macOS has no ML-DSA in .NET 10 (Claimed)

.NET 10 validation callback (Tested). Copy the server-sent intermediates into ExtraStore when you rebuild the chain, or the build fails:

c.ChainPolicy.TrustMode = X509ChainTrustMode.CustomRootTrust;
c.ChainPolicy.CustomTrustStore.AddRange(roots);
foreach (var el in ch!.ChainPolicy.ExtraStore) c.ChainPolicy.ExtraStore.Add(el);
bool ok = c.Build(cert!);

Server side

nginx: ML-DSA and ECDSA side by side (Tested)

ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/pki/mldsa-fullchain.crt;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/pki/mldsa-leaf.key;
ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/pki/ec-fullchain.crt;
ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/pki/ec-leaf.key;
ssl_ecdh_curve      X25519MLKEM768:X25519:prime256v1;

OpenSSL picks the certificate from the client's signature_algorithms. OpenSSL 3.5, Python, Node and .NET clients got ML-DSA; Go, Java and OpenSSL 3.0 clients got ECDSA. Key exchange stayed X25519MLKEM768 (or X25519 for OpenSSL 3.0). Full configs for other web servers: Web servers and proxies.

Apache httpd, HAProxy, Envoy

Apache accepts several SSLCertificateFile / SSLCertificateKeyFile pairs and HAProxy loads multi-type bundles, but neither was tested with ML-DSA here (Unverified). Envoy uses BoringSSL; ML-DSA serving not confirmed (Unverified). AWS load balancers cannot serve ML-DSA.

AWS Private CA

CLI flow (Documented values; not run here, no AWS credentials):

aws acm-pca create-certificate-authority --certificate-authority-type ROOT \
  --certificate-authority-configuration '{"KeyAlgorithm":"ML_DSA_65","SigningAlgorithm":"ML_DSA_65","Subject":{"CommonName":"Example ML-DSA Root"}}'
aws acm-pca get-certificate-authority-csr --certificate-authority-arn $CA --output text > ca.csr
aws acm-pca issue-certificate --certificate-authority-arn $CA --csr fileb://ca.csr \
  --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_65 --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/RootCACertificate/V1 \
  --validity Value=10,Type=YEARS
# get-certificate, then import-certificate-authority-certificate to activate
openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-DSA-44 -out leaf.key
openssl req -new -key leaf.key -subj "/CN=svc.internal" -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:svc.internal" -out leaf.csr
aws acm-pca issue-certificate --certificate-authority-arn $CA --csr fileb://leaf.csr \
  --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_65 --template-arn arn:aws:acm-pca:::template/EndEntityCertificate/V1 \
  --validity Value=90,Type=DAYS

Private CA copies the SAN and public key from the CSR without validating them, so build the CSR carefully. A subordinate CA must use a key algorithm its parent supports (both Documented). Terraform and CloudFormation are in Full configuration files; whether your provider or resource schema version accepts ML_DSA_* is not confirmed (Unverified).

AWS KMS (ML-DSA signing, not TLS)

aws kms create-key --key-spec ML_DSA_65 --key-usage SIGN_VERIFY
aws kms sign --key-id $K --message fileb://msg.bin --message-type RAW \
  --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 --query Signature --output text | base64 -d > sig.bin
aws kms verify --key-id $K --message fileb://msg.bin --message-type RAW \
  --signing-algorithm ML_DSA_SHAKE_256 --signature fileb://sig.bin

Documented. Use it for code and artifact signing or as a KMS-backed CA key; it does not put ML-DSA into TLS by itself.

Composite and hybrid certificates

  • Composite ML-DSA for X.509 (ML-DSA plus RSA or ECDSA in one key and signature) was published as RFC 10073, Proposed Standard, November 2026 (Documented, datatracker).

  • .NET 10 has a CompositeMLDsa API that moved to draft-08 at GA (Documented, Microsoft Learn); check it matches the RFC before use.

  • OpenSSL 3.5 composite support: not confirmed (Unverified). AWS Private CA lists no composite algorithms.

  • The ML-DSA TLS code points (mldsa44 0x0904, mldsa65 0x0905, mldsa87 0x0906) come from draft-ietf-tls-mldsa, still a draft; OpenSSL 3.5 already sends them (Tested).

  • Until composites are widely supported, dual certificates (ML-DSA plus ECDSA) give the same fallback without a new format.

The CLM product's role

The CLM codebase already has ML-DSA plumbing: certificate policy (clm/internal/certpolicy/quantumsafe.go), HSM signing (clm/internal/hsm/craton_mldsa.go), the Nitro enclave signer (nitro-enclave/internal/pqc/signer.go), and composite and hybrid certificate tests. These were found by file name; the code paths weren't reviewed.

Split of responsibilities:

  • ML-KEM: discovery plus runtime and config fixes (the rest of this document).

  • ML-DSA: a CLM re-issuance campaign. Start with internal mutual TLS, service-to-service and code signing; public endpoints wait for the web PKI. CLM should issue the ML-DSA and ECDSA pair together so servers can run dual certificates.

Steps

  1. Finish ML-KEM rollout first; it protects against the urgent threat.

  2. Inventory certificate signature algorithms in CLM, starting with long-lived roots and intermediates.

  3. Build an ML-DSA hierarchy beside the existing one (Private CA or CLM) and add its root to every client trust store.

  4. Pilot dual certificates (ML-DSA plus ECDSA) on one internal mutual TLS path. Expect OpenSSL 3.5, Python, Node and .NET clients to take ML-DSA, and Go and Java to stay on ECDSA.

  5. Expand per path, keeping the ECDSA certificate until every verifier on the path negotiates ML-DSA.

  6. Public certificates when CA/Browser Forum rules and browsers allow.

Packaging per compute type

Clients need the private root in their trust store; servers need both key pairs.

ECS/Fargate, EKSDebian 13 or Alpine 3.24 base; root into /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ + update-ca-certificatesnginx (Debian 13) with both pairs from Secrets Manager or a mounted secretTested (nginx, clients); update-ca-certificates with an ML-DSA root Unverified
